It. is hoped that the inquiry will not extend beyond the present year.

The connection between Australian mutton and the unity of the Empire might seem to be somewhat recondite. Mr. Hogan thinks otherwise, and Mr. Powell Williams agrees with him. The War Depart- ment, it appears, has offended the patriotic pride of Australia by labelling its raeat as fereign. Mr. Hogan in a fine burst of rhetoric, called upon the Depart- ment to " restrict the use of that phrase inifuture to meat coming from beyond the boundaries of the Empire." As a Liberal Unionist Mr. Powell Williams was bound to sympathise with the senti- ment of Australia 83 interpreted by Mr. Hogan. Nevertheless, there was a suggestion of mock gravity in the phraseology of his reply. "Consider- ing the universal feeling that exists in favour of the unity of the Empire," he solemnly declared, " we shall be careful in future not to speak of meat coming from the colonies as foreign." The House laughed in the spirit of an audience that has assis• ted at a capital bit of burlesque.

--- Lord Salisbury's continued indisposition is naturally causing much uneasiness at the present Juncture. A mors inopportune moment for a re- arrangement of high State offices could scarcely be imagined, and it is by no means probable that any immediate development of the kind is in contempla- tion. Nevertheless, the old rumours of impending changes at the Foreign Office are again t beginning to make themselves heard. The cause is not far to seFk. The Prime Minister's reputation as a master of diplomacy in foreign affairs has suffered total eclipse in the estimation of many ardent Conserva- tives. There is a feeling abroad that, while Lord Salisbury's colleagues may hint vaguely at the possibility of a resort to war, Lord Salisbury him- self would never consent to the terrible arbitrament, and it is suggested that his notorious disposition to keep the peace at all costs is encouraging foreign Powers in a policy of deliberate self-aggrandisement at the expense of British interests.

The growth of tipping in London—once half- resented as an alien custom imported from France —has certainly outetripped the land of its birth. Even co the Londoner,who picks his way discreetly it is a great, and apparently a growing, infliction, while to the stranger it naturally suggests scarcely veiled highway robbery. A recent Canadian visitor has been enlightening his fellow colonials upon its baneful extension and universality. Our over-the- sea friend boldly alleges that he tact only one man in London who refused a tip, and he was a guard at the Bank of England. "If,' be says, "I had not left my kodak behind I would have taken his pic- ture." There is a conclading anecdote of a sarcas- tic character in this connection :—" As our grand ship Canada was about leaving Liverpool landing- stage, one of our passengers, holding a handful of change, shouted out. "If there is any man,woman or child here that I have not tipped since I have been in England, I am prepared to do it now !" It is certainly time that a stand was made against the practice, and an Anti-Tipping Association ought to have a future before it.

WHkT THE SWEEP SAID. A lady who owes probably bee life, certainly her health and happiness, to a sweep who same to her house" on business," has been visited by a " Newark Advertiser " reporter. For fourteen years, Mrs. Pegg (of Cethare, near Newark) had been through the fires of affliction. "For twelve years," she said, I was like a woman three- parts dead." She had a combination of conaplaints, chief " of which were a very bad digestion and a torpid fever. She could not digest ber food, and every meal used te bring on severe a pains. Her blood became Impoverished, doctors could do nothing for her. "I cannot refrain," said Mrs. Pegg, "from expressing the great gratitude of my heart. For fourteen years I suffered much. So weak did I become that to walk up- stairs gave me very great difficulty, and I had to gasp for breath. Whatever I ate caused me intense suffering, and I soon became unable to do my work ; life was a burden to me. One day,when our sweep came to clean the chimneys he noticed how ill I looked, and he said, 'Why don't you try Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People?' I had tried nearly every medicine advertised, and the doctors could do me no goucl, so I had little falth in anything. However, after talking it over with my bushaad, we determined to give the pills a trial. That is three years ago now,and you would hardly know me for the same woman. The first box began to do me good, and, persevering with them, I quickly got quite well. Dr. Williams' Pills have done wonders for me; there is nothing like them. They are our family doctor now. Whenever I feel run down, instead of sending for the doctor, Ity to Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People." The old, unscientific days, when all family medicines were simple purgatiee pills or mixtures, are gone by. It is recognised that an aperient is only a temporary remedy ; the medicine that is to cure must cure not symptoms but the Callst's of disease. Dr. Williams' Pink Pills, the safest and most universally useful family medicine ever compounded, are not a purgative at all. They strengthen, instead of purging and weakening ; hence their world-wide celebrity for the cure of ansemia rheumatism bronchitis, asthma, consumption and de, ecrefula, and chronic erysipelas. They are also a splendid nerve and spinal tonic, and thus have cured many cases of paralysis, locomotor ataxy, neuralgia, Sr.. Vitus' dance, and nervous headache. It is necessary to take care not to take a substitute ; pills coloured pink in imitation of Dr. Williams', and sometimes actually called Pink Pills, are offered by some otherwise respectable tradesmen. Not one person was ever cured by a substitute, however : therefore do not be deceived into paying for anything that does not bear the full name, Dr. ,ms' Pink Pills for Pale People, on the wrapper. In case of doubt it is better to send I direct to Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, 46, Holborn. viaduct, London, E.G., 'Deming Price, 2s. 9d. for one box, 13s 9. for six. " It is good to be Dennis's wife she exclaimed. " Bow I wish it were possible for me to make him happy—intensely happy! But when he discovers all I shall be lost—lost!" She covered her face with her hands, aa if to shut out the sight of her new possessions. Just then a cab drove up in front of the hone( . A moment later Grace heard the click of a latchkey in the front door, quickly followed by the sound of men's voices in the hall. She knew at once that her husband had returned and brought Eric Hume home with hire.

The drawing-room door stood open, and she could hear them talkin together in that free-and- easy manner which amlounces a well-tried friend- ship. "We shall be quite alone; my wife has asked no one else," Grace heard her husband say. "I'm very glad of it," was the reply. "I don't know how it is, but I can't get the thought of that forged cheque out of my mind," continued Dennis, lapsing into an anxious tone. "I'm afraid it will prove a nuisance and bring me no end of bother."

"It's unlucky for you that your name was the one selected to be forged. Now, if it had been mine, there would have been no balance to meet it, and the whole affair would have been simplified." "The thing is a confounded nuisance! I expect shall be dragged into giving evidence against the Y:ri i nal, or criminals, on some inconvenient day, knd have my name appearing in connection with a case which will bring me neither cash nor kudos. I regret now not having paid the fifty pounds, irstead of saying the signature was forged, and calling upon my bankers to pay up. I only wish I had an inkling who committed the forgery. I should know better how to act then." _ _

"I wouldn't let the matter bother you so much, old man," observed Eric stoically. What's the use of it? You should look upon the affair as one of those trials to which the holy-minded bow with resignation,' as your aunt, Mrs. Hughes, would say." "It's all very well preaching, but I'm not holy- minded." As Dennis said this he led the way upstairs. "Make the best of everything, good and evil alike, is my motto," answered his friend, following him.

To every word Grace listened with a strained, agonised expression. But as Dennis and his friend entered the room she came fcrward mechanically to meet them, striving to appear composed. "Here we both are, Grace!" exclaimed her husband, adopting a cheerful tone. Eric took her extended hand with a feeling of keen surprise. He had expected that she would be a handsome woman, of the full-blown peony type, and with an aggressive manner. He was totally unprepared to see a refined, sweet-looking and lovely girl. Lovely was the only word ap- plicable to her, so he forthwith decided. In- stantly his usual frank manner asserted itself, and he determined to forget that his common- sense had revolted at the precipitate manner of his friend's wooing. He was glad he was ignorant of the pros and cons of the affair, and made up his mind to exonerate Mrs. Vane from all blame. She was probably a victim to circumstances. Possibly she possessed cunning relatives, who had planned this hurried marriage for her. He had previously determined that it should not cause a breach between him and his old friend, and that decision was now strengthened many degrees. For a short time conversation was restricted to ordinary topics. The weather was discussed, and the Vanes' trip to Germany referred to. By a violent effort at self-command, Grace succeeded in making appropriate answers to questions addressed directly to her. But she made no attempt to become discursive. She longed to escape from the presence of others, and to have an opportunity for debating with herself how she ought to act with regard to a secret which lay heavy on her mind. Meanwhile, Eric wondered if she was always so quiet and incapable of becoming inter- ested in what was passing around her. "Vane has heard a strange thing to-day," he observed, with a view to arousing her attention. "His name has been forged to a cheque." "Forged !" repeated Grace, not looking up. "How did yon hear of it, Dennis?" "I was going through my old cheques to-day and came upon it," replied her husband. "For how much is it drawn ? " she asked, look- ing down. "For fifty pounds. The signature is almost the pa,sine.lsn iffactht,e Idatbeelhieavde nlotshboeuelnd •Ifiacav-simile que written in a different handwriting. It was that which first attracted my attention ; then I com- pared the number of the cheque with two others bearin, the same date, and I found it must have been taken out of another book." "All this seems difficult to understand," she said in a hopeless voice. "I am not good at business. Who is supposed to have written the signature? " "No one has the ghost of an idea, Mrs. Vane," observed Eric, who now regretted having brought up the subject. Happily, at that moment dinner was announced. Nothing could have created a more opportune diversion, so thought Eric, as he offered his arm to Grace. But his sense of relief was small in comparison to hers. With a feeling of having just escaped from a trying ordeal, she took her place at the dinner-table. Later in the evening Eric decided that for one so young, his hostess had a peculiarly careworn and troubled face.

DOESN'T CARE FOR LEAP YEAR.—She snapped her fingers disdainfully. "That for leap year! " she said. "I wouldn't give one common year for a whole bushel of them." "Perhaps," said her dearest friend, with that solicitude for which dearest friends are noted, "someone has given you the mitten." "Not at all. He jumped at the chance to get me, and we're engaged." The dearest Howl suggested that she didn't see just what fault could be found with leap year under those circumstances, the complaint usually coming from girls who had made a trial and failed to score. "Why, there's nothing artistic about it," explained the engaged girl. "ft isn't sportsmanlike to bag your game that way, and there's no real excitement or fun in it. Just a little nervousness and it's all over. Any girl can ask a man to marry her, but it's more of a trick for her to make a man ask her. That calls for careful and artistic work. My '95 engagement was twice the sport of this affair. IT MADE A DIFFERENCE.—" Then you do not love me?" The young man's voice had a tremor, but the girl heeded it not. In fact, there was no reason why she should love him, if she didn't want to. " Alas ! no." "Then you will not marry me?" "Why, of course—what on earth has thas to do with it?" she asked. And would you let your wife read your MS. before you sent it to the papers?" she asked. "Would I' Why, I'd let her help me write it." It is announced that 500 new buses are about to be launched upon the crowded thoroughfares of bondon. Congestion in the leading lines of traffic can hardly be carried farther. At some points the crossing of streets is a matter of supreme danger or of excessive delay to pedestrians, and the new pro- gressive Council and the City Corporation have be- tween them a fine opportunity, by mans of a series of overhead bridges, of justifying their existence. By midnight every 'bus will have disappeared from the streets, and not one of the 500 will probably ever think of instituting an all-night. or even half- night, service. lam told that the all-night half- hourly service of trains which was lately com- menced by one of the local railways is very success- ful, and that other lines are about to give the public similar accommodation. But the question of suc- cess is one on which the railway managers are en- titled to be beard, and a six months' profit and loss account on the all-night trains may have a disagree- able story to tell.

There has been nothing in the commercial history of recent years to equal the rush witnessed within the last few days for shares in the newly-formed Lipton company. Many have been the applicants, few in proportion the recipients. Although the issue was for two millions and a half, not a meagre amount, the public were willing to subscribe to the extent of double and triple the sum. The offers received up to the present reach un aggregate of nearly eight millions. It is understood that a cer- tain proportion of the shares will be reserved for allotment to applicants who are interested in the maintenance and expansion of Sir Thomas Lipton's great business.

The idea that the Secretary for the Colonies is restless under the conditions attending the present leadership of the Unionist party has been encour- aged by an incident which occurred ol Monday evening at question time in the House of Commons. When Mr. Balfour was asked about the proposals with regard to the West Indies,he replied, in effect, that the Government could give no information on the subject, but was instantly followed by Mr. Chamberlain, who, without being asked proceeded to give the House considerable information, at all events as to why the proposals were not forthcom- ing. It is only a tew days ago that a similar inci- dent occurred as between Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. I Curzon. It is possible, of course, that the Colonial ' Secretary acted merely upon impulee,but it is indi- cative of the unrest which exists in the House that incident' of this kind should be closely watched and interpreted in a sensational fashion. There is unquestionably a growing belief on the Unionist benches that Mr. Chamberlain is chafing under what the" Forward " party regard, and are openly de- nouncing, as the " weak " foreign policy of Lord Salisbury ; and while this belief exists the Colonial l'ecretary can hardly be surprised if exaggerated importance is attached on his own side of the House to actions which may of themselves be insignifi- cant enough

-- There are four points of danger at present to the peace of the world, and the breaking out of war at any one of them would lead to it probably at all the others—supposing, at least, that Great Britain could be made to appear as the offending party. The war clouds are gathering more ominously than ever over the situation in the Far East, and the franco- Russian protest against the Angio-Garrnan loan,and the accompanying demand for territorial cempen- sation by France and Russia, coupled with the re- fusal of Russia to leave Port Arthur, may be the spark which may kindle the conflagration. In the Franco-Russian demands there is an end to Lord Salisbury' fiction of the integrity of China ; but if Britain were dragged into war in the Far East she would be embroiled also with Abyssinia and the Transvaal. In West Africa Russian and French in- fluence is strong enough to alarm Menelik,or to ex- cite his covetousness and ambition, and could, therefore, put his armies on the move. It could also she up the Boers to seize the opportunity for shak- ing off the so-called suzerainty of England, and be- coming the predominant power in South Africa,and, lastly. a single shot in the Far East would set both thei Frenchi and British in West Africa into a blaze. This s n reality the danger that confronts us.

When Mr. Gladstone brought grocers, licences into existence he was credited with having inven- ted a new and perhaps a dangerous trade. The feather, such as it is, was plucked from his cap on Wednesday by witness before the Licensing Commission, himself a man of some note,combining in a single personality the dignities of commeree, learning, literature, and laws. Mr. Alexander Walker, L.L.D., J.P., grocer, wine merchant, anti- quarian, and author, was quite willing, if members of the Commission had been of the same mind, to trace Mr. Gladstone's legislation to a mediceval source. "I could take you back to the twelfth cen- tury with it," be observed invitingly, " but perhaps an instance from the reign of Mary Queen of Scots will suffice." The Commission being of opinion that that would represents sufficiently respectable anti- quity, Mr. Walker proceeded to fulfil his promise. At the famous battle of Harlaw, be informed his hearers, one of the combatants was no less a person- age than the Provost of Aberdeen. In private life this magnet was a grocer, and at.cording to Mr. Walker he held either a grocer's licence or its six- teenth century equivalent. Thus privileged, the citizen soldier, with true Aberdonian shrewdness, turned his wars to comm.rcial account by supply- ing comrades in arms with liquor. At Harlaw, for example, be stimulated the general courage, and at the same time did a thriving trade for himself, by carting hogßheads of claret into the battlefield.

"This is most extraordinary news! " ejaculated Mrs. Hughes. "Most extraordinary!" she repeat—. in a higher key. "That Dennis should married in such wild haste surprises me beyond words. I really do not know what to think of it! But I can scarcely believe it is true. Let me read the letter, William." "Here it is, my dear. Unfortunately, the news is only too true," he replied dismally. "Poor dear boy! Entrapped by some cunning girl, or her relations. It is quite heart-breaking! Are you not very sorry? I am." "I am indeed—both sorry and disappointed." "You should have returned with him to England when that telegram arrived at Les Avants. You do not seem to have given the matter a moment's thought." "Had I imagined he was hurryinc, home to get married, I should have given him advice—which there is not the remotest chance he would have accepted. Young men—London men especially— do not think that the advice of a country clergy- man is worth anything. But it's of no use regretting the past." , "None whatever," concurred his wife dolefully. "Take some buttered toast, William, before it gets cold. Do eat a good breakfast. You have a ten-mile drive before you. Dennis says his wife is the daughter of an olEcer—of course she's the same that Mrs. Hicks told me about. Poor dear boy! We ought to have taken better case of him. Unfortunately, there is nothing we can do, now." "But make the best of what cannot be undone. put in her husband. "Yes; that is the only thing we can do," agreed Mrs. Hughes, with a deeply-drawn sigh. "After all, the girl may prove a good wife." "She may. All things are possible in this world. But girls who marry in unseemly haste very seldom do make good wives. It really is too disappointing! I was so fond of the dear boy. I always pictured his marrying a charmingly sweet girl, and having a grand wedding." "We won't discuss matters on those lines, Maria. He is married, and has evidently married rashly. We will not desert him at such a moment. Probably he never wanted our advice so much as now."

"Yes; we will be true to him. He will have been married a month to-morrow. He has actually taken this house at Cam pden Hill and furnished it without letting us know anything about it I should think very strangely of the whole affair " here Mrs. Hughes's voice sank almost to a whisper—"if he did not say that he felt sure I should like his wife; for Dennis knows my tastes, and so she must be a nice, quiet girl."

it )(es." _ "Military people are often very flighty. Have you forgotten how disgracefully Captain Hope's wife flirted with all the men who came within her reach—even with you, my dear? It was for every- one's good that she left the neighbourhood. Bu about Dennis. Of course, we must tell Mrs- Floxham and the Grangetowns, and Meredith and all the people he knows down here, that he is married." "Yes; the sooner they know it, the easier it will be to avert a family scandal," agreed Mr. Hughes. "But it would be very foolish to let them know that we have not seen Grace. Everyone w ould instantly form their own opinion of the marriage, and say most unkind things about it. We must act cautiously, William, and try and make people think that everything is satisfactory. After a l we have no positive proof that it is not. "Neither have we, Maria. But it will be hard to induce our friends to believe that a secret wedding, which was concealed from us for a month after it had taken place, is one of which we can fully approve." "This is what I suggest. Let us go up to London at once, make the acquaintance of Dennis's wife, and stay with them." "Supposing they do not want our society ? " "Of course, they will be delighted to see us; and on our return home we will tell everybody where we have been staying, and that Dennis is married. I shall be able to describe the furniture and Grace's new dresses, and distract the women's attention from the actual wedding day. Don't you understand ? " "Yes. You're a diplomatic person, Maria." "If my being diplomatic can help dear Dennis tc hold up his head in the world, I'm glad lan diplomatic—not only for his sake, but his dear, dead mother's." "It's always wisest to look at matters from their brightest point of view. When do you suggest our going to London ? " "To-morrow. There's no time to be lost." At the same moment that his uncle and aunt were taking this lenient and kindly view of his wedding, Dennis was facing the trying ordeal of divulging his marriage to °Eric Hume, the latter having called at his chambers to announce the fact of his own engagement to Constance Treherne. Dennis was quite prepared to hear this piece of news, and he offered his warmest congratulations. But talking of the Trehernes did not encourage a spirit of contentment with his own prospects. Just for a moment he found himself recalling Gwendoline's clever, lovely face and her keen powers of sympathy. "So you're spliced out-and-out spliced," remarked Eric, carefully knocking off the end of his cigar. "Yes; we shall have been married a month to- morrow."

"A month to-morrow! Then your wedding followed close upon the heels of your hurried return to London ? " "Yes." Dennis spoke in a manner which inferred a hope that his friend would not ask any more questions. "Well, old man, I wish you no end of haiarAe ness," said Eric thoughtfully. "Thanks." Then, as if anxious to divert the conversation from his own wedding, Dennis said: "When do you imagine you'll be married? "In about a year's time, I suppose." "What are you doing to-night? Will you come and dine with us ? "
"I'm engaged to-night. May I come to- morrow instead?"

"Yes. We dine at half-past seven. No. 5, Castletown-villas, is the address." "It ie always just as well to know the address of the hom3 where you're going to dine," rejoined Eric with a smile, turning to go. As he walked down King's Bench Walk, his face became overclouded. "He's been and made a fool of himself, has Vane; I'm sure of that," thought he. "Of all the blind asses! However, its not my affair. Looks about five years older already. I shall be interested to see this modern siren who he has married. By Jingo! one would have thought a strong-minded fellow like he is, would have been proof against that kind of fascination. One can't help pitying him, though. Poor old chap! "

div.head: CHAPTER XV.
div.p: CHAPTER XV.

Grace was in a flutter of excitement, compara- tively speaking, for it was the first time they had entertained a friend at dinner; and the meat, idea of acting hostess was alarming, especialxv Dennis's greatest friend, of whom she stowr unaccountably in awe. She was very ignorant of etiquette, and being anxious that nothing should occur which might reveal this fact, she had pur- chased a book on the subject that very morning, and had spent the greater part of the afternoon studying it. A yearning to consult her husband had been judiciously suppressed, though she had longed for his advice, especially in the choice of her dress for the occasion. After much cogitation she had decided on wearing a black lace gown— one which he had helped her to choose. As to jewellery, she only possessed his wedding presents, an artistic gold necklace and diamond marguerite. The moment she was fully attired she scanned her appearance critically, and, for the first time in her life, with admiration. She realised that she was pretty with deep thankfulne4. "I am glad t" she murmured happily. "Dennis Vane's wife ought not to be ugly." As she entered the drawing-room she gave a final glance round. Was everything well arranged? she asked herself. It was an artistically furnished room ; warm, subdued colouring pervaded through- out. Although everything was new, yet it possessed a cosy appearance, rendering it a pleasant room in which a tired man could spend his even- ings. Grace was commencing to love her pretty home, and to take the rast pride in its arrange- ment.

div.head: CHAPTER XVI.
div.p: CHAPTER XVI.

Grace Vane looked the picture of misery, as she leant back amongst a profusion of soft pillows in her pretty drawing-room. From time to time, when there happened to be a temporary lull in the traffic, she could hear the two men talking and laughing in the room below. She wondered what they were talking about, and how Dennis could be merry; for she knew he keenly resented his name having been forged. Then she thought of Eric Hume, and hoped he would not stay late. If, after he was gone, her husband brought up the subject of the forged cheque, then—perhaps she might find courage to tell him the truth. But she was not allowed much time for brood- ing over the troubles that were coiling themselves around her.

"Aunt and uncle Hughes have just come!" exclaimed Dennis, entering precipitately, and speaking with genuine satisfaction. "They are in the dining-room. I thought I had better come up and prepare you for seeing them, as you looked so ill during dinner. Do you feel all right now ?" "Oh yes, thank you. I was not feeling really

"I'm awfully glad they've come!" he continued. just like them, though, coming up post-haste to put matters straight and to hear all the news. They are the kindest-hearted people going. You are 'sure you feel equal to seeing them ? " "Oh, yes—quite.' But Mrs. Hughes had not the least intention of being treated ceremoniously in her favourite nephew's house. Without waiting f)r his return to the dining-room, and notwithstanding Mr. Hughes's undisguised disapproval, she deliberately mounted the stairs and entered the drawing-room. _

"And this is your wife, Dennis? " he ex- claimed, walking up to Grace and shaking hands most cordially. "Dear me! How strange it seems to find you a married man! It was only the other day that you were trotting about, a dear, lovable little darling, in white frocks and a blue sash. But I have not quite forgiven you yet for marrying without my consent. However, I am thinking of forgiving you goon." "You have done so already, aunt," he replied with a laugh. "Don't be certain—don't be certain," she answered, endeavouring to speak severely. "I am so pleased to see you, Mrs. Hughes.' said Grace in a low voice.

"And I am delighted to meet you," she answered in her most agreeable voice, surveying her new niece with a feeling of surprise and satisfac- tion. Then she continued, speaking in her usual quick, emphatic manner: "You must have been married more than a month, and your husband .anly let us know about it yesterday! .1: did not believe before that he could keep a secret from me 40 long. You have a very pretty home," she added, glancing round, thinking it best not to dwell tco much on the secrecy of the wedding, "and the best of husbands—of that I am quite sure—for Dennis is a man in a million! "

"Hear, hear," observed the person referred to. "Now, really, Dennis. you must desist from those boyish ways of treating serious matters as 3okes! Married men should be staid and thought- ful • not given to levity at all times." "He'll become staid and thoughtful quite soon enough," said Mr. Hughes, who happened to enter at this moment and overhear the remark. _ .

Dennis immediately introduced his uncle to his wife, and Mrs. Hughes added a few observations, which clearly pointed to the fact that she had already seemed a certain degree of proprietorship over C;rare. li.deed, if the rood lady had cared to tioaly:e brr ieviii:gs towards her netkew'e bride,

Eric Hume acted a silent but observant part, well satisfied that his friend's married life was beginning under better auspices than he had Ventured to hope would be the case. _Conversation drifted on pleasantly and smoothly. Mrs. Hughes started an aside chat with Grace on domestic Subjects, dear to her heart. She compared the price`bf butter, eggs, sugar, rice, &c., &c., as ticketed up in London with that payable in the country. She was delighted to find how well versed Grace was in such matters. Little did she imagine how deeply the latter had been forced to study this branch of economy:' 'ln due, course tea was brought in, and she criticised most favour- ably a cake which Grace owned to having made herself.

- ------ "So you ate really quite a domesticated character," she observed in a charmed voice. "Dennis," she continued, turning to her nephew, "you must bring your wife down to stay with us very soon. We shall be killing ayig shortly—" "Pray don't trouble to kill it on our account!" he interrupted, laughing. "We shall make our- selves quite happy without an attraction of that kind." .

"-I was about to observe," said Mrs. Hughes, "when you broke into the sentence, that I would give you a aide of bacon to take home with you." "Thanks awfully, aunt!" Dennis spoke with keen appreciation. Never before had he known his aunt to part with a side of bacon which had been cured at the Vicarage, and he knew that this present should be regarded as a great compliment. "About those Trebhernes," began Mrs. Hughes, whose aptitude for jumping from one subject to another was startling., "I have often wondered what became of them—and you, Mr: Hume—after we left Les Avant& "

"We went to Chamounix together." "Oh indeed ! " Mrs. Hughes's manner of saying it conveyed more curiosity than surprise. Hume has the. felicity of being engaged to Constance Trebenae,'' observed .Dennis. "Really!" ejaculated Mrs. Iftighei, looking at Eric in a manner which revealed she was momen- tarily at a loss what else, to say. . "I offer you my sincere 'congratulations," Ob- served her husband, coming forward opportunely. "Miss Constance Treherne appeared to me a very charming young lady, and there can be no doubt that she will make you an excellent wife. Will you kindly tell her that my wife and I wish you both every happiness?""Thank you, said Eric. "I will tell her with pleasure, and I am sure she will be very gratified at your kind message." Both men were conscious of having said the right thing at the right moment. Of course, Mrs. Aughes kneW ' she was expected to -add a supple- !anent to her husband's congratulatory • BMA. After, a moment's consideration she observed: • "I am very glad you are engaged. Mr. Ilume• It is always pleasant to hear of a young man thinking seriously of marriage. It shows he has a sincere desire to lead a respectable, law-abiding life. You both have my best wishes for your happiness." . "Aunt evidently thinks very badly of the life --you are leading now, Hume,' said Dennis in an under-tone. -
Mrs. Hughes felt that under the 'circumstances any further reference to the Trehernes, would be quite out of Place, so she plunged into a'discussion on dress.

"I really must buy myself a new bonnet," Ate said to Grace. "I wonder if you could come shopping with me to-morrow, and help me to choose one? Willirrn is of no assistance to me in that way. I went into a shop this afternoon and tried a bonnet on. When I asked him if it suited me he said he really couldn't tell, but that if it felt comfortable on the head I had better buy it. Then he asked the 'milliner if it was lined with cork!" _ .

appeared •to me a very natural remark to make under the circumstances," said Mr Hughes, noticing that the others smiled. "A very practical, sensible obeervation, uncle— one that I can easily imagine your making," said Dennis. "You evidently Wok an 'interest in the stibject." "So. I did, for the Moment,. concurred his uncle. "Really, Maria," he added aside, "we must not stay any longer this evening. We are keeping these young people up." , "Then ,shall I call for you to-morrow morning, or will you join me at our hotel?" said Mrs. Hughes, addressing Grace, as she began drawing on her gloves. "But you mustn't stay at an hotel. You must come and stay with us, aunt; and you too, uncle," put in Dennis. "I shall be very pleased if you will,* added Grace. "And then we can have several days' shopping together." "Of course we can," observed Mrs. Hughes, very satisfied at the Course events were taking. "It will give us much pleasure to come and stay with you. Having Dennis as our host will be quite an amusing novelty. Then we'll come to- morrow, if it's quite convenient." "You can't arrive too soon," observed Dennis. A little more discussion as to the hour of arrival, &c., and the matter was settled. As Mr. and Mrs. Hughes were driving back to the hotel a few minutes later, the former observed thoughtfully "I wonder, Maria, if we shall ever know the exact history of Dennis's marriage and the history of Dennis's wife—but I like her. "My dear William, pray forget that there such a thing as history. The future of these young people .is what we must think of, not Grace's history. You and I must try and smooth their life's path for them by taking them in hand now. It will put down all slanderous reports and make the whole difference to their position in the future. I feel quite certain that the girl is good and that she is devoted to Dennis. They are married. We must make the best of it." "Yes—yess you're right," agreed Mr. Hughes: land she is a very ladylike person and attractively pretty," (To he continued.

A great improvement in the roads has been made in the Berlin district, which example might be followed with great benefit to the cycling public by the English authorities. Bicycling tracks nine feet wide have been laid down on each side of the ordinary road, so that cyclists need never meet each other as they must always ride on the right-hand track, nor are they allowed to ride on the ordinary causeway. This plan causes the danger of riding to become much lees, and to timid riders it is an especial boon. div.head: SOCIAL PROBLEMS. FARM COLONIES FOR. THE
div.p: SOCIAL PROBLEMS. FARM COLONIES FOR. THE
UNEMPLOYED.
By JOSEPH FIYDER, General Secretary of thr Land Nationalisation Society.
ARTICLE XVIII.

Instead of saying, as hitherto, that the duty of the State towards the pour is to find the necessaries of lite for all who need them, we must say that it is the duty of the State to provide the poor with an opportunity of earning these things. HERBERT V. MMUS (" Poverty and the State.") Not only you in England but a great part of the world, Imitate some ill mastery that are readier to chastise their scholars than to teach them. There are dreadful punish- ments enacted against thieves, but it were mach better to make such good provisions by which every man might be put in a method how to live, and so be preserved from the fatal necessity of stealing, and of dying for it.

_ SIR THOMAS MORE (" Utopia.") Passing by the workhouse (pleasanDy named, because work cannot be done in it). I saw sitting on wooden benches in front of their Castile, some half-hundred or more of these men. They sat there, near by one another ; but in a kind of torpor, especially in a silence, which was very strik- ing, . , An Barth all lying round, crying. "Come and till me, come and reap me" ; yet we here sit en- d:l'l2w I „ • "Do not look at us. We sit enchanted here, we know not why. The Bun shines, and the Berth calls, and, by the governing powers and imix)tences of this England, we are forbidden to obey. It is impossible, they tell us P There was something that reminded me of Dante 's hell in the look of all this ; and! rode swiftly away, THOMAS CARLYLE C' Past and Present.") I have alreaey given expression to my convictions that the whole unemployed difficulty is the outcome of a simple initial wrong which denies to labour that free access to the source and foundation of all employment which it ought to enjoy. But as it will probably take some time for the nation to realise this fact and to courageously act upon its knowledge, something has to be done meantime in order to aid the many thousands of honest and willing workers who are noes compelled to be idle.

TRN POOR UM EMITILLISS. No serious effort has yet been made by the State to deal with the problem. The question " bristles with difficulties," say our timid statesmen, as they excuse themselves for their Antutterly inactivity. "No man need starve," they say. "Is there not the workhouse ? And do we not pay £10,000,000, a year in poor rates for the support of the unfortunate people who cannot support themselves ? What more can we do ?" Certainly tea million pounds is a goodly sum. If wisely nen: it could surely accomplish much mare than it dues now. But the nation is not getting best sn.lue tor its money at be present time. The workhouse system has assuredly broken down. To use an expressive Old Testament phrase, it is beginning to "stink in the nostrils" of those who know its working best. It is apt to treat poverty as a crime, and paupers as criminals. It is governed grudgingly (as a rule) by the guardians of the rates,who are facetiously styled guardians of the poor. And yet it is costly, in spite of all their striving for economy. Out of every pound paid by the ratepayers for the support of the poor no less than ten shillings (in many cases) are absorbed by the mere expenses of administration. Some of the most needy sine deserving it entirely fails to reach. With the intentional degradation of its pauper uniform, it heartless separation in old age of those whom " God has joined," and its other prison like fea- tures, is it any wonder that men and women often choose to die rather than seek the cold hospitality of its gloomy walls and surrender themselves to its tender mercies ? Yet the fault lies not so much in the Poor Law itself as in the spirit and nuihod of its administra- tion. And it is probably by means di the Poor Law (whea Improved) that we shall have to settle the unemployed on the land.

div.head: GOOD BUT NEGLECTED ACT.
div.p: A GOOD BUT NEGLECTED ACT.

And here I may say that an existing statute empowers Boards of Guardians to acquire as much as 50 acres of land,and to employ thereon the poor who seek relief. But, for reasons that are easily understood when we re- member the class of individuals who have generally managed to get thems,lves elected, this power has lain unused for so long that it is now obsolete. It did not commend itself to tho vowerful trinity of Hedge's mas- ters—the squires who owned the lard, the farmers who hired the squires.' land, and the State clergymen who who were appointed to their "livings " (significant word !) by the lords of the soil. Squire and squires par- son sat together on the bench to mete out justice (of the rustic sort) to landless vagrants and poachers. And tbs squires farmers joined them at the Union Boards. But their highest idea of relieving the poor was to dispense doles of " eighteenpence and a loaf" to th labourers whose wages had been "kept back," as St. James said, "by fraud "—by the fraud that robbed them of their birthright in the land. The old-fashioned Boards, and there are hundreds like them in force to-day, could con- ceive of no better labour test than stone-breaking or oakum-piclsicg. So they wouldn't use the best power which Parliament had conferred on them, and I don't know of any case in which the legal 50 acres were ac- quired. So the Locel Government Board has vetoed a proposal that was recently made by a Board of Guar- dians to avail itself of this ancient statute. The reason they give for their refusal is that the Act is absolete. I entirely disbelieve the reason assigned. The antiquity of an Act ought to be no argument against it. It ought to be possible for Boards which are sufficiently enlight- ened to obtain land for farm colonies instead of setting men to drudgery and comparative uselessness of break- ing stones and picking eakuns.

From time to time attempts have been made, outside a Poor-Law, to deal with the unemployed. Private in- dividuals as well as religious and philanthropic bodied have taken land for the purpose. In conjunction with the experience gained by the Labour Colonies of Holland Belgium. and Australia the results are instructive. Mr. Walter Haze% M P., took a small farm in Essex, and he received 109 cases in four years. The material was bad. Forty-four of them came from common lodeina-houses or refuges. Scarcely one had a trade or had belonged to a trade union. But they were trained in farm work, strengthened with good food, and improved by regular habits. And then the majority were assisted to farms in Canada where most of them turned out well. One excellent feature of this colony—now removed to a larger farm at Chesham, in Bucks—is that there is no barrack system, but the men are treated kindly as men of a family. The Salvation Army Farm Colony at Hadleigh, in Essex, founded in 1891 as a part of the Darkest England Social Scheme, iv a more amtlitious endeavour. It contains about 1,200 acres, and about 2,000 men have passed through it. A large sum of money was spent in founding varieuS Industries, but they have involved a heavy loss. Ex- perience in such matters has always to be bought at a heavy price. Whatever the final result may be, thS Salvation Army deserves every credit for its plucky effort to rescue the "submerged tenth," and it has, I consider. at an excellent example to other Christian bodies. Though, after all, the main work will have to be done by public bodies. Neither religious nor philan- thropic bodies can cope with a natural problem of such magnitude. Acotber interesting experiment was made by the Mansion House Committee on the unemployed. They selected 141 out of 414 applicants. Of these 141, 94 were Londoners by birth, and 17 others urban. Thus it will be seen how it is the weakened townamen rather than the incoming countrymen who chiefly swell the ranks of the unemployod. The men were set to work on London County Council land at Abbey Mills. As only 14 were dismissed for idleness or misconduct, it was clear that there was a general willingness to work. The general results were satisfactory.

THE STARETHWAITE COLONY. But .he most hopeful experiment of all thus far made is the Rev. Herbert DElla's Colony at Starnthwaite, near Kendal. Not by reason of its size, but because of the principles upon which it is founded and the intentions of its founder. To gain an adequate idea of his scheme It would be necessary to read his book "Poverty and the State" (Regan Paul, Trench, and Co.). Ho wants " co- operative estates" to be formed by the Boards of Guar eians, and he believes that they could be made substan- tially self-supporting. He goes into full details in sup- port of his views. He would put every man to the work best suited to him. For the work done no money would be paid, but a good home would be provided,good meals supplied, and serviceable clothing, in which a Liberal choice of design and material would be afforded to the workers, in place of the uniform ugliness which aCCOM. panics the present system. And there is one more im- portant point of the scheme which I would emphasise— viz., four-fifths of the work should be done for use and not for sale. He gives the case of the West Derby Union, in South• West Lancashire. It keeps au average of 2,000 paupers every week in the workhouse, at a coat of £4OO. Outdoor paupers receive an average of 3s. per week each, amounting to £350. The actual average cos{ in direct relief is thus £39,000 a year, but other ex• peuses increase this to £50,030 a year ; and this is exactly doubled by the average expenses of collection and distribution. Thus the Union pays £lOO,OOO a year. Such a sum would amply start a colony in which the able-bodied residents could at least support thernselveS by their own labour. It is in this directien that ireee, we shall have to MOTO. The Starnthwaite is a privately-conducted illustration on a small its practicability. But it has, unfortunately, been hampered by lack of funds.

The manner in which fashion rebounds from one extreme to another is well seen at the present moment. We have worn blues and greens, violets and reds, till the streets and park have looked like gay parterres of moving flowers. Now We go in for all the neutral shades imaginable. Grey is still in the running, but is quite second to drab, stone colour, fawn, beaver, and, above all, "putty." That sort of soiled white or dingy cream is all the rage. No one can call it pretty, and it certainly is not useful; but fashion disre- gards the fitness of things and decrees that it shall be worn, though of course, it will soon give way to something else.

Russian fashions, it is almost neealess to say, 'hive invaded the domain of evening attire, and :a.ost of the bodices are pouched, and generally open in front over a full, bagged front of some soft material or lace, while the blouse is outlined with trimming round the neck and down the fronts. Dahlia and bright peach lints are employed for evening wear, combined 'with akin lace, bright plum or violet tinted velvet, and marrow beaver fur. div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

During the Queen's stay at Windsor it was noticed that her Majesty experienced much less difficulty in welting that has been the case for some time past. Wte n proceeding to ilietant parts of the palace a wheeled chair war used it is trite, and in order to reach the gal lere f the private Chapel on timiddy r, • ice chair was necessary for the steps thet ii.tervene- between tbe level of the cell idor and that if the ro yel pew, but the Sovereign was able to eesilv maeaeran all short distances aided only by the arm et the I i.dia at- tendant. The private Chapel at Windsor Castle was the favorite music room of George IV. It is lighted by cil lamps, poised in a central pendant, and the handsome service of gold plate was presented by her Majesty soon after the commencement of her reign. Morning prayer is said in the Chapel every morning of the week while the Court is in residence, but with the exception of each Sunday the Queen rarely attends. The gallery is s trictly reserved for the use of her Majesty, and it can only just be over looked by the preacher. Princess Margaret of Connaught, whose confirmation ook place in this chapel the other day in the presence tf the Queen and several members of the Royal Family, alias just entered her seventeenth year. Her Royal High- ness inherits the name, and also the bonny vivacity of her roother,whaas many of my readers will doubtless re- member, is a daughter of Prince Frederick Charles, of Prussia. Princess Margaret is admittedly the most prac- tised and enthusiastic ef all the royal cyclists in this country, and a a great favourite with her grandmother —the Queen. The marriage of Princess Marie of Greece, who was with het father, King George, when the attempt to as- sassinate him was made,is, according to preretit arrange- ments, to take place this year. Her fiance, the Grand Duke George Micheillovitch, is an officer of Horse Ar- tillary,andata aide-de-camp to the Czar. Two years ago the date of tbe wedding had practically been fixed, but owing to the disasteous Greco-Turkish war, the royal nuntials had to be indefinitely postponed. It wriaild seem probable that orthodox bridal dress will shortly be ceunted among the niodes of the past, for many brides of late, have appeared at the altar clad in dainty pretty frocks that would be useful afterwards without necessarily ticketing them as brides. So far however, they have retained the usual veil as well as flowers, which is a wise proceeding on their put, as there is nothing like a veil for etherealizing even the most material bride. Bridal wreaths nowadays are almost exclusively com- posed of orange bloisem on a background of maidenhair fern a sprig of stephanotis here and there blending its exquisite fragrance. The hawthorn was the flower which formed the wreath of Athenian brides, and the bridal wreath of the Roman woman was of verbena, plucked by the bride herself. Holly wreaths were sent as tokens of congratulation, and wreaths of parsley and rue were given under a belief that they were effectual preservatives against evil spirits. Out of every thousand women in this country, forty- eight, it appears, sign the marriage reeieter with a cress implying that they are unable to write. The proportion Is small, as compared with what it was a quarter of a century ago, but it ought, nevertheless to be smaller. A leendon Clergyman atated, a week or so back, that be recently performed two marriages, in which the brides —both under twenty years of age—made their n.arks, on the ground that they could not write, and doubtless many clergymen could tell of similar instances. To he exclusively French, it is necessary now to have change of hair for different times of the day—for light, and artificial light. Many fashionable women, well-kneavn in Society, indulge in the brightest auburn —a most becoming colour—for evening wear, but Inas- muoh as this particular trurpee makes them look ghastly by daylight, a harml(se and not very telling. brown is donned in the day time. Really hairdressers nowadays,must be makingthandsome fortunes. It is not every woman of course who cares to change the colour ot tier artifice! tresses, but the women who refuse to avail themselves of the advantages for a tourpee, are at the moment, few and far between. Belts in future, are to be in the same colour as the costume. The old jewelled variety are being sold off cheaply, which is their sentence of extinction. All the new bodices are pointed at the waist in front, and the belt should follow this line. By putting the Paterham or other belt material oiagoually through the hers of the buckle, and firmly sewing it there, after the correct ' angle has been ascertained, this idea can be easily carried out. In blouse silks, the new periwinkle blue is to be one of the leading colours this spring, and coming summer, but it is not everyone who will be able to wear this par- ticular tint to advantage. The average run of more or teem sallow people, will have their defects accentuated ' by its delicate brilliance. To blouse silks,plaid patterns, tiny checks, and Bayadere stripes will all be worn. Many of the large plaids are inspired by the Scotch tartans, 1 but the tiny checks are in cerise, green, periwinkle, porpy red and grey, with fine white and black lines. Spinning wheels are now frequent additions to the furniture of a boudoir or drawing room. A good many girls learn the craft, and spin well, the knowledge that they look pretty at their wheel being no doubt a great inducement. Another fashion is the harp. Those who do not play the instrument like to see it in their rooms. But the music itself is becoming very popular,ever since the Queen was so gracious to the Miss Esslers, at Balmoral. 1

In the quaint little town of Winchelsea, has bean re- vived the ancient industry of lace making. The little town with its silent cobble-paved streets, set apart on a little bill between rail and sea, is just the sort of place where the click of the lace bobbins seems most at home. The lace made is simple, but it is very strong, and is admirable for underclothing, doylery, or children's pil- lows. It is made with very fine linen thread and looks as if it would wear for ever. . .

According to a well-known complexion specialist, a few s;rnple precautions in youth would defer wrinkles many years. Women should avoid tears above all else. There is a lining to the membrane of the muscles around the edge, which contains water. By crying, this wate is lost. The supply is not equal to the loss, causing r dryness of skin, which produces wrinkles. Gentle mas- sage is an excellent thing, but one should be careful to always rub the sane way. Even the lines in the fore. head can be rubbed away, if one is patient enough. • good complexion powder lightly dusted on the skin is beneficial, and pure soap containing no alkali is non. injurious, and should be used daily. Excessively hot water dries the skin and wrinkles it, while cold water stimulates and refreshes it. The first lines usually ap- pear between the ages of 25 and 28 years. If they come before they are usually caused by illness or mental die. tress. At the period mentioned the natural secreticns of the flesh begin to recede, leaving the skin too large for the space it covers. This is what causes wrinkles.. _ . .

Here lathe recipe for a dainty sweet. Take half a pound of apple pulp,a quarter of a pound of granulated sugar, an ounce of bntter,two eggs, the grated rind and juice of one lemon. Pare, cors,cut up and boil sufficient apples to make half a pound when cooked. Add to these the sugar and batter which should be melted, and the eggs be&ten up. Stir the mixture well. Lastly stir in the lemon juice and rind. Line a at tart tin with paste and spread the mixture on it.put on in the same way as you would jam. Bake for about twenty minutes in a good oven, It may be served hot or cold. MADGE."

div.head: STRANGE DEATH OF A WARRINGTON FORGEMAN.
div.p: STRANGE DEATH OF A WARRINGTON FORGEMAN.

Mr. S. Hrigirouse,coroner, held an inqueirt at the Police Court. Warrington, on Wednesday morning relative to the death of Thomas Laish, 70 years of age, a boiler maker, of 2, Hale-street, who died at the Infirmary on Monday. Ann Leigh. wife of deceased, said the latter was 70 years of see. A few weeks before Christmas, he had an accident at Hallam forge. When became home later in the day he said be had slipped end cut his knuckle on a plate. For a fortnight 'be went to his work but his knucklelept swelling. He then went to Dr. Adams. Froin that time to the 4th February, he was off work entirely, and on that day be went to the Infir- mary. In answer to the Coroner, Mr. T. Atherton, sub- manager at the works,said they had no official notice of the accident at the works. They had heard that he fell when leaving the works at 5.30 p.m. He did not know the date of the accident. They had no direct evidence that he had had a accident, and only his own statement to a follow-workman.

Dr. Langdale, senior surgeon at the Infirmary, said deceased was admitted on January 7th for a few days and then went home. tie had an inflamed hand ,and re- turned on February 4th, and remained in the Infirmary until his death on Mcnday.Desth was due to exhauation consequent upon the inflamed hand. Practically speak- ing it was a case of blood poisoning. Dr. Adams, said that deceased came under his care some time in November, or the beginning of December. "Wittics was the surgeon to the forge. When he came to witness his right hand was swollen and he said he had fallen and there might be some glass in it. As he could not be properly attended to at home witness suggested that he should go to the InArmary. All he said was that he bad fallen. The condition of the hand could not have arisen without injury to the hand. Nurse Hill said that deceased died at 1 p.m, on Mon- day in the Infirmary. During the time he was in the Infirmary he made no statement as to the cause of his pnjury to her. ThP Coroner said that from a legal point of view death was duo to th- exhaustion consequent upon the blood. poisoning. They had very meagre evidence that the in- nry WAR due to an accident. If the man was insured or £l,OOO at would be very serious to hay that it was uP to an accident. The jury, after about 20 minutes deliberation,returned a verdict to the eff-ct that deceased died from exhaus- tion set up by a wound,but how that wound was caused there was no evidence to show.

A FIRE BRIGADE OFFICER.

Capt. W. Howlett, Chief Officer and Secretary to the Jockey Club, Owners' and Trainers' Fire Brigade' Fire Brigade Office, Wellington Street, Newmarket, has just written :—"Withgreat pleasure I send you this unso- licited testimonial. For thirty-twoyears I have been a member of Fire Brigades, and the last twelve years chief officer. I have tried all sorts of Cocoas, for often called up in the middle of the night to attend a fire one re- quires something to stimulate and stay the stomach, especially when getting soaked with water and choked with smoke and steam. Nothing I have ever tried has done me so much good as Dr. TIBBLES' VI-COCOA. It makes me fit for anything, hawever fatigued at or af:er a fire."

div.p: TIM F r: P.-IMA/, MARCH 11, 1898.
A WARRINGTON TELEGRAPH INSPECTOR KILLED.

A railway accident,which was attended with fatal re- sults. happened on Tuesday morning on th rsilwtc near St. Helena Junction. It appears that Soh-Inipecter F. Bourne, who was employed by the London and North- Western Railway Company as telegraph inspector of the Warrington district,which includes St. fielens,was mak- ing an inspection of the wires crossing the Liverpool maim line near the Junction Station when be was knocked down by a passenger train, and received such I injuries that he died within an hour. Bourne was a ' single man, aged about thirty. His parents lived at Fennel-road, Higher Broughton, Manchester, but Bourne had for some time lodged at Warrington. The railway company are about to carry out extensive alterations In regard to the telegraph lines and arrange- ments at the Junction, and Bourne was on Tuesday morning taking particulars of the existing lines. The alterations to the wires, km, are to be made in connec- tion with an enlargement of the station which the rail- way company are about to commence. The platforms are to be extended and raised, and other improvements I which have long been desirable are to be made. In the course of his duties Bourne had to cross and re-cross the main lines between Liverpool and Manchester, and also the line leading from the main line to St. Helens. At 9.47 the express train from Manchester to Ft. Helens passed through the station. The driver,Henry Meadows, of Peasley Cross, had slowed down in order to go safely through the points and round the curve, and when the locomotive got to the end of the platform Meadows whistled for the deceased to clear the line,and as Bourne appeared to be unconscious of danger, John Gibbon, the signalman in the box close by, went to his window and shouted. Bourne, however' did not notice anything until the engine was close upon him, and before he could step out of the way the buffer caught him in the cheat and knocked him some distance along the tine, Re alighted with his head on the rails and it was cut severely, while the poor fellow's left foot was run over and mangled. Plate- layer Johnson and the men working near,at once ran to Bourne's assistance, and the engine-driver pulled up in a very short distance. The station-master, Mr. Lueae, at once sent for Dr. Casey. Bourne was carried on to the platform, and seeing that his injuries were extremely serious, first aid was rendered by the station staff, and the unfortunate man was put on the 9.40 train from Newton to Liverpool, that was standing in the statism, land taken off to Liverpool. Thanks to the promptitude of Mr. Lucas, Bourne was on his way to the Northern Hospital within five minutes of the accident occurring. Mr. Lucas telegraphed to the hospital for the ambulance , to meet the train at Liverpool, but Bourne succumbed to I his injuries soon after reaching the hospital.

div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
THE CUP COMPETITION.

The sub-committee governing the Cup Competition met in Manchester on Monday night. Mr. J. E. Warren (Warrington) was in the chair, and the others present were E. Gresty (Broughton Rangers), J. E. Langshaw (Runcorn), H. H. Waller (Briehouse Rangers), H. Hut- chinson (Wakefield Trinity),A. Fattorini (Manningham), and J. Platt (Oldham) secretary. The matter of the Leigh and Heckmondwike dispute was again under dis- cussion, the charge being one by the Yorkshire club that Leigh had not given them suffi- cient facilities for checking the gate in their cup tie. The committee were dissatisfied with the explanation given, and suspended two of the Leigh officials from exercising any official capacity in connection with the Leigh club. Mr.Renton,the referee in the match Broughton Rangers v Wakefield Trinity, reported Cleminson, of the first-named club,for illegally charging an opponent, and he was suspended for one month. The following officials were appointed for the third round of the cup, to be played on March 19 : Cast Word v Batley : Referee,E. Holmes (Manningham) ; touch judees,J.Latham(Wakefiald Trinity)and W.Robin- son (Manningha.m). Huddersfield v Broughton Rangers : Referee, .1. 11. Smith (Widnes) ; touch judges, A. div.head: SOME "SCORES."
div.p: SOME "SCORES."

The Ireland of Sir Jonah Barrington's day is fruitfu in witty memories. Sir Boyle Roche,generally so genial, had a hard saying in rerly to Curran, who was declar- ing that he needed no help and could be the guardian ofl his own honour : " I always thought the honourable gentleman was an enemy to sinecures." Curran, how- ever, was not to be attacked with impunity, and, some time later, when Sir Boyle was boasting that Sir John Cave respected him extremely, and had given him big eldest daughter, Curran struck in : " And, if he'd had an older one depend on it, Sir L'oyle, he'd have given you her." There is an amusing story, too, of a barrister's score off Lord Norbury who bad s great name as a hanging judge. "I am reminded,rny Lord," he said, " of a judge I once beard of, who never wept but once,and that was at the theatre." "Some high tragedy.! suppose, Mr. Grady P" fe Not at all,my Lord: It was at the Beggar's Opera, when they reprieved Mace heath." The first Lord Plonket established at the Irish Bar a reputation f3r wit which his descendants have not let die out. Many are the roofs of his on rectard ; one of the funniest relates to Lord Campbell, who was coming over to supersede him in the Chancellorship. The weather was rough,and some one happened to remark that the passage Must have made him very sick of his promotion. e, I'm afraid," said Lord "that it won'! have :Rade him throw up the seals." Contemporary sayings are little available for an article of this kind, as they can seldom be published without offence. There is a witty dean who might fur- nib our pages, but one example of his ingenuity mus suffice : An unhappy gentleman opposed hien in debatt ngle: have vde. Thec. c t at an ecclesiastical meeting, heedless that his name lent Itself to puns. The Dean interrupted hie speech by say- ing "that he did not think he had given Mr. Brush any handle for such a sweeping ass,' don." This is a very temper, elaborare piece of verbal wit ; but sometimes the simplest and moat obvious wordsre toartreed i fri e e aly Not long ago two undergraduates were arguing at Ox- ford, result of a happy elythe sadtil and one questioned w o losingar gumhei ne t "Oh," the vary "any advantage ve foolbest tn stca score re 0f can a .n s ra sometimes ri see that.'"f There you acci- dent, rand its owner may acquire reputation by a fluke. Two Senators in America were speaking their mind to one another with all the customary freedom." "I believe upon my comscience," said ene at last, "that you are the greateqt rascal unhung," " Sir," retorted the other, spluttering with rage, " you forget yourself." Happily there were bystanders who caught up the inot and ap, plauried, or its inventor would never have known of him crushing score—From Of 'Scores,' " in the " Cornhill Magazine" for March.

div.head: P RUDE N TIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY.
div.p: THE P RUDE N TIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY.

DISTRIBUTION OF £lOO,OOO AMONG THE STAFF The directors of the Prudential Assurance Company, y way of celehratine trio jubilee of the company and recognising is some way the zealous and loyal services of their staff last year r-cemtnended the shareholders to set aside eut of the surplus of 1898 the sum of £50,000, and this year have added an equal sum, making a total of £lOO,OOO. They have arranged a staff (about 15,000 in number) according to duration of service, as a Jubilee bonus. Fifty pounds will be the maximum in any single case. They have also established a fund called the Pru- dental Staff Provident Fund, to which members of the outdoor staff wh-, have been with the comp toy at least a year and whose income in Itits than a certain amount, will be invited to contribute 21 per cent; of their earn- , ings each year, to which the company will add a sum of 50 per cent, and upon the amount standing to the credit of contributors interest will be allocated each year. It Is one of the best features of the scheme that contribu- tion to the fund is to be entirely voluntary. This scheme was uuanimously approved at the annual general meeting of the Prudential, at which some stag- gering figures were given as to the general growth of this colossal corporation. For exantple : In 1868 the assets were £218,409. In 1898 they are £30,438,337. The income of the company from premiums alone is seven and a half millions of money for the past year,and out of the forty millions of people in this country no lets a proportion than thirteen millions are insured ia the Prudential.

To illustrate the widespread character of its operations the Chairman gave these curious facts :—The company has paid 17 claims for lives lost in the recent frontier war in India. Of nine persons drowned in the capsizing of the surfboat at Margate, six held policies in the Prez- dential.Of the four firemen burned to death in the recent catastrophe in Glasgow all were insured with this corn- psny. The Maidstone enidernic caused the death of 132 persons, of whom exactly half 86, were insured here. The surplus for the year amounted to £1,631,825, out of which, after carrying forward the sum of £641,736, £lOO,OOO was to be added to the reserve fund. The local superintendent for the Prudential is Mr. J.T.Rowiarel.
SERIOUS FIRM FIRE AT WINWICX

A farm fire of a serious nature occurred at Winwick Ott Monday night. At 10.10 Inform ition was received at the Fire Brigade Station, Warrington, to the effect that a fire had broken out on the farm premises of Mr.Joilepk ,Swinton, Arbury Farm,near Winwick. No time was lott in starting for the scene of the conflagration, Mr. Frank Turner,deputy superintendent, and his men taking with them the steam fire engine Major. When they arrived at the farm they found the fire burning fiercely, and they at once directed their efforts to extinguishing it. They continued hard at work for about seven hours. when the outbreak was got under. No less than twenty tons of straw. 2.50 bushels of oats, and 25 tons of hay,of the value of £3OO were destroyed. The damage to the out-buildings is estimated at about £3OO. The buildings are insured. The cause of the fire is at present enveloped in mystery. It was discovered by Mr. J. W. Kaowles, who at once gave the alarm and roused the workmen, who, with the assistance of the neighbours, did all they could to put out the flames until the arrival of the fire brigade. There was a good supply of water.

MARCH ll'h, 1698:

THE Stepney election which has The Stepney Election. resulted in the gain of a seat by the Liberals was in some respects the most important and suggestive electoral con- test that has taken place since tho General Elec- tion. The Conservatives held the constituency for twelves years, and there seemed to be no reasonable prospect of the Liberal candidate being able to wipe off the adverse majority of 472, es- pecially as the list of voters is not a large one. But, as a matter of fact,not only has the majority been rubbed off but the Liberal has been returned to Parliament with a balance of twenty votes to his credit. The special significance of the election is to be found in the indication which i. affords of the change of political feeling in London. As far as the Liberal party is concerned the metropolis hasbeen and, indeed, is yot, one of blackest of the black spots on the electoral map of the country. But the Stepney election, like that at Waltham- stow, seems to promise that there will be a very marked change in the representation of London at the next general election. It shows, too, like Walthamstow, that the candidates who may be selected to win metropolitan seats for the party of progress must be of a downright democratic stamp. Mr. STEADMAN who has just been returned to the House of Commons is a representative London workingman and takes his plac• in the very front rank of the Radical wing of the Liberal army. This eloction, like those in connection with the London County Council last week, can be regarded as nothing less than a vote of censure by London electors on the Government On the Liberal side it has,according to all accounts, been contested with extraordinary enthusiasm, workingmen, in particular, having thrown them- selves into the struggle with quite exceptional ardour. No doubt many of these voters have been influenced almost entirely by labour questions, but there can be no doubt that the election also voices the disappointment, not to say disgust, caused in the country by the general policy of the Government. In foreign affairs, for instance, matters seem to drift from bad to worse. Indeed one almost begins to think that this country has now no settled foreign policy at all. When Min- isters are questioned about the development of events in West Africa or in China, it is as likely as not that two versions of the same incident will be given—one in the House of Lords by Lord SAmsnuay and another in the House of Commons by Mr.Ounzoi.r. These curious contradictions have happened so often that even usually well-informed people appear to be now quite at sea as to where this country stands in regard to the West African and the Chinese questions. Until within the last few days it was universally believed that the policy of the Government so far as China, is concerned is that of the "open door," to quote the briefly convenient ' phrase that is now in fashion. In other words, it was believed that our. Government had finally and irrevocably adopted the common sense plan of abstaining from any land grabbing in China, but of at the same time insisting that, whenever any other country established authority over parts of China, the right of free • and open trade should be maintained. It was believed, too, that Lord SALMI:MY had obtained definite promises from both Russia and Germany, that they would not interfere with freedom of trade in the Chinese dominions. But later news does not confirm these comfortable theories. It is now asserted that Russia has demanded from China the concession of sovereign control over Manchuria, and it is well-known that wherever Russia exercises absolute authority there foreign trade is, as a rule, annihilated by prohibitive tariffs. It appears, too, that Russia has made nO very definite promise with respect to freedom of of trade, and that our Government has therefore not even a Russian promise to rely upon for the protection of British trade in the Est. The re- velations and rebuffs which follow each other leo quickly have apparently about convinced the people of this country that their affairs, foreign as as well as domestic, are in the wrong hands. He has allowed Greece, one of the most topeful:of these struggling communities, to be depressed and degraded and has in this way helped to pave the road of Russian ambition. He and the country which will he represents are now suffering from the diplomatic weaknesses of tke Vast, and as soon as the electors thoroughly realise this fact many other seats will, like that for Stepney, be handed over to the Liberal party.

The relations between th The United States and Spain. United States and Spain seen to have taken a decidedly awk- ward turn. There has been no official report from the officers who were deputed by the Government at Washinon to enquire into the causes of the destructivn of the war-vessel Maine at Havana, but somehow or other there now seems to be a disposition to conclude that the report will be of an adveise character—in other words that the vessel was blown up by a Spanish or Cuban torpedo. It has been foreseen all along that such a report as that would raise a storm of indignation in the United States and lead to demands being made upon Spain which that country may not willingly con- cede. War wouid be then practically inevitable. If the latest reports be correct the Governments of both countries now feel that a peaceable settle- ment of the points of issue !s becoming more and more unlikely. Preparations for a naval conflict are, it is said, being pushed forward with the utmost energy both by the States and by Spain. War vessels which have just been completed, or are about to be completed, in the dockyards c,f Europe, are being purchased by one Power or the other when possible, and war material of other kinds is being accumulated at the various arsenals. If war must come, there is

in this case the satis;action of knowing tl2at the conflict will be short and sharp. Probably the first naval encounter of any magnitude will settle the matter. If the United States can Obtain the ascendancy at sea tl e chances of Spain continuing the war with any promise of success would be extremely remote. On the other hand, if the Spaniards succeedeciiu crippling the American fleet—which is not at all likely—it is difficult to see what advantage the United States could expect from prosecuting the contest at the present time as more warships could not be built for months to come. Without a fleet that was able to command the seas it would not be possible to drive the Spanish troops out of Cuba. In the end, howeve:, the United States are bound to prevail.

There s one point which should not be lost sight 0; at tee mpeucuug election of Guarliana for the Warrington Union, arid teat is in reference to the Assessment Committee witich is appointed by the Guardians. The public have a right to ask the can - didates who seek election the'r position with refer- ence to the assessment of public houses in the Union. It is patent to all who have followed the subject that public-houses are assessed at a redicu- lously low figure in Warrington, and that the com- mittee either suffers from a lack of system in deal- ing with this class of property as they increase in value,or that the members are unwilling to face the difficulties which naturally arise. It is a well- known fact that the population of Warrington is increasing at a rapid rate—it is now about 63,000— but still the number of licensed houses re- Mains the same. It therefore naturally follows that the turnover of these houses is increased by the larger number of inhabitants, and consequently that they are of more value to the owners. It is almost unnecessary to paint out that if one sectioa of the ratepayers is too lowly assessed, other sec tions are unjustly called upon to pay au unequal share of the rates. This is a matter which affects 11l classes, audit should be ventilated at the ensu - bag election of Guardians.

An incident in which tragedy and comedy were ftllinily commingled occurred at Latchford on Wed- ariiiday afternoon. Somebody—it's as well to be ague—made.the startling discovery that a corpse 'Was floating on the waters of the Ship Canal, and raised the alarm with a promptitude which would have won praise from the Coroner had that official Ultimately been required. A knot of enlovirers was Soon formed,and the body was carefully scrutinised from every point of view for about an hour. Then the ship Canal diver and the local constable appeared on the scene and assumed command of the modus oporandi for effecting a rescue. The constable, with praiseworthy cuteness,gave orders that the corpse must be landed on the Cheshire aide of the waterway, and a boat was promptly launched, manned, and propelled to the spot where the semi-submerged body floated. By now the spectators had so increased in numbers as to far exceed the legal definition and meaning of "a crowd," and excitement was intense. With grave mien,and tactics reverential, careful,and cau- tious, the rescue party angled for the object of all tbe "to do." It waa hauled on board, proved to be S sack, and msnifestly contained something mor material than spiritual. The covering was cut off, and all that remained mortal of a diseased-looking canine was exposed to view. Cursory remarks from the water's placid surface,and long prolonged beers from the bank, terminated an incident which Will be memorable in the minds of at least a few.
Under tke Wild Birds Protection Acts, the Cho- hire County Council gives n3tie• that the taking _ _

or killing of wild birds is prohibited in the county of Chester from March 1 to August 12. All right- thinking people will commend the ruling of the Act, which prevents the extermination of our feathered songsters by that branch of pleasure- eeekers carrying a shot-gun,and labelled sportsmen. The wild tirds are of no use dead, while alive they enhance the charms of Nature, and particularly in rural Chesnire, to a very large extent. This is all the argument required for the justification of an order prohibiting their ruthless destruction. In 411othet column we publish particulars of the order and the parishes it effects, but the penalties of its infringement are vaguely, but none the less deter- rently, referred to only as those "mentionad in the eaid Acts."
