div.p: RUNCORN LEAGUE OF 'ME CROSS..

The weekly of the above was held on Sunday night in the League Rooms, Irwell-lane, the president, Mr.. William Woods in the chair. The Chairman gave some miscellaneous readings as also did the chaplain,the Rev. F tther Gore, which were highly appreciated by the large audience. The usual votes of thanks brought the muting to a close. •

Ban .zsna7P.S.A. The usual weekly meeting of the above P.S.A. was held in the Runcorn Congregational Church, on Sunday afternoon. The afternoon's speoker was Mr.A.BAthbate of Garston, who delivered an appropriate address. The soloists were Miss A. Cooke,who gave a fine rendition of " T.e Chorister " ; Mr. Ambrose Shingler's interpreta- tion of " A Dream of Paradiss " was ercellent, whilst Master F.Lowe,of Widnes,also contributed a solo. There was a very large attmdance. The membership now stands at 154.

THEFTS BY A FOREIGNEE AT RI, NCORN. Carl Leyon, a Norweigan sailor, was remanded by Mr Ockleston at the Runcorn Police Court on Thursday morning, until to-day on charges of stealing an auto- harp valued 124. 61. on the 15th January, the property of Ada Churchill, Waterloo-road, Runcorn, and also with stealing a pair of boots valued 93. 61., the property of Arnold Unsworth, second-hand chthes dealer, Percival- lane, Runcorn, on the 14th January.

div.head: RUNCORN PICKWICK CLVII
div.p: RUNCORN PICKWICK CLVII

At the meetin-g- of the Pick-WiCli-Ciu-b-o-n Tuesday even- ing a paper was read by Mr. J. A. Hayes,entitled "Cari- cature and Caricaturists." The essayist compared the caricaturists of olden times with those of to-day, and said that in his opinion, th,?sa of t( day cou;d not boast of sny superiority over those of days gone by. He gave illustrations of both, by Enlarged sketches taken from examples of each school of caricature, amongst others being several of caricatur.n in stone which he had taken from the originals which are to be found is some of the old churches up and down the country. He also gave some illustrations of modern caricatures amongst which were some of Gillray and Cruikshank. The essay was received by the audience with thorough apprecia- tion.

ALLFGED FALSE PRETENCES BY A SAILOR. At the Runcorn Police Court on Saturday morning bo- fore Mr. James Handley,John Richard Marshall, a sailor was charged on remand with stealing is. 6& by means of a trick from John McMahon on Thursday. The evi- dence given was to the effect that Marshall came from Liverpool on Thursday and mat the prosecutor in the Marine:a' Hotel. On the representation that the prisoner bad signed as ship steward on board the Cashier, lying at Saltport, which he wai to join on the itth March, the prosecutor gave him is. 63. Prisoner influenced McMahon by a note purporting to have been signed on behalf of the captain of the ship by " Swinton." As the prosecutor was not present, Marshall was remanded in custody for a week. THE ALLEGED THEFT FROJI WESTON POINT SALT WORKS. At the Runcorn Police Court on Friday, before Mr. W. Timmins, William Johnson, of no settled abode, was charged en remand with stealing a watch and chain,the proprrty of David Walker, from the Salt Works at Wes- ton Point, on the 24th February,—The evidence which has already been reported, was repeated, and as the watch had not been recovered, the charge was with- drawn.—Prisoner was then charged with wandering abroad and lodging in the Salt Works, without any visible means of subsistence.—P.C. Bancroft stated that when he apprehended the prisoner on the charge of steal- ing the watch,he replied "You have got no witnesses to prove it." Prisoner,however,admitted that he had slept on the works.—Johnson was committed to prison for 14 days' hard labour. RUNCORN ST. PAUL'S MEN'S BIBLE CLASS. Mr. R. H. Posnett presided over the monthly meeting of the above class held in the morning ckapel,on Sunday afternoon. After the meeting bad been opened by hymn and prayer, Mi. Pilgrim gave a very sweet and clear rendering of " Native Worth" (from Haydn'e " creation ") Miss B. Harrop was listened to with rapt attention during her interpretation of " Tired." Mr. Reading of Northwich, delighted the audience with his rendition of "I dream of Paradise." " The Better Land" was sung by Mrs. Temperley with good feeling, and Mr. Reading sustained the interest by a most powerful and masterful rendering of " The Holy City." " Carry me back to my mother's home" was charmingly sung by Mrs. Temperley. The afternoon's programme concluded with the rising, 'Eternal Rest" by Mr. Pilgrim.

John Thomas Trelfer, a s9aman, was remanded by Mr. James Handley, at the Runcorn Police Court on Saturday, until to-day (Friday) on a charge of stealing 50 fathoms of rope, the property of Joseph Shallcross, of the Snasfell. The evidence adduced showed that the flat Snaefell was lying opposite the " Big Houses" at Runcorn on Thursday night. A number of ropes were left on board. The next morning the prosecutor missed 25 fathoms of three-inch rope, 12 or 14 fathoms of four inch rope, and a small handy rope which had a hook attached.—Ralph Atherton of the flat Sarah, stated that on Thursday night prisoner came and asked him to lend him a knife. HO said he wanted to cut a rope. Witness lent him the knife and subsequently saw him working with it in his hand. CAUGHT IN THE ACT AT RUNCORN. -

At the Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday, before Mr. Walter Timmins, Enoch Rolleston,a boatman,of no fixed abode, was charged with stealing two pairs of boots from the shop door of John Tyler, Bridge-st., the previ- ous day.—P.O. Gregory said he was on duty in Bridge- street on Monday afternoon, about 12.30, when he saw the prisoner coming down the street. When he got to Tyler's shop he put his right hand up and snatched the two pairs of boots (produced)from the doorway and put them under his arm and walked away quickly up High- street. Witness followed him and took him into custody.ln answer to the charge he said "I have nothing to say,"—Charles Harris manager of Messrs. Tyler's shop, said the boots produced belonged to his masters. He saw them safe about 20 minutes past 12 o'clock the , previous day. They were hanging on a nail in the door- I way. In consequence of hearing a noise at the doorway witness looked out and saw Rollestm deliberately snatch the boots away and walk off.—Prisoner was committed to the Knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial. CLAIM TOR PROFESSIONAL ATTENDANCE EY A RUNCORN DOCTOR. At the Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes,Dr. Ormsby,of Runcorn, i claimed a guinea from James Jolley,tinsmith, Bridge-st. Buncorn,for professional attendance on his wife.—Percy Wright, secretary to the Halton Ladies' Club,stated that the defendant's wife was a rnembn of the Halton Female Friendly Society, and when a doctor attended a confine- I ment cas3 he was entitled to charge his usual fee. The point had never been before the club, but it had always been understood that an extra charge should be made in such cases.—Dr. Carruthers said he had been doctor to this society for twelve years, and assistant ler ten years under his father, and they always charged their usual fee for such cases.—Dr.Ormsby also gave evidence as te attending the defendant's wife during her confine- ment. Witness told them that his fee was a guinea.—The defence was that the rules of the socie:v covered the case.—The judge gave judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed. His Honour observed that defendant was unwise in disputing the matter. CONCERT AT THE SEAMEN'S .MISSION.

On Tue;Ki-e-v-eniag at the Seamen's Mission a large and appreciative audience assembled to take part in the, evening's entertainment provided by Miss F. Graham of Moseley Hill,and party. The items were well rendered and provoked much amusement. The following was the programme :—Song, "The March of the Cameros Men,' Mr. G. Cunningham ; comic song, " Mrs. Gattem," Mr. W. Orton ; " Soldiers of the Queen," Mr. T. Lunt ; comic sketch, " The Absent Man," Messrs. C. A. and F. Tunnington and E. Gibbs ; trio, " A Little Farm well Tilled," Messrs. G. Cuuningham,R. Morris,aud T. Lunt; song, " Afton Water," Mr. G. Cunningham ; " Hoax, Coax, and Jokes," Messrs. C. A. and F. Tunnington ; song, " The Boys of the Old Brigade," Mr. T. Lunt ; comic song, " Where have I seen that face before," Mr. W. Orton ; sketch, "Paddy's Mistakes ; or the Gordian Knot," Messrs. G. Cuuningham,T. Davies,J. Goodior, T. Lunt, and L. Morris. A vote of thanks to the artistes for their admirable entertainment brought the evening to a close.

HALTON-ROAD WESLEYAN CEOIE—ANNISAL "SOCIAL." On Wednesday evening; last, the Halton-road Choir (winner of this year's Widnes Eisteddfod) held their annual social.a large number sitting down to tea. After tea, games were indulged in, followed by a programme of music. Song, "A Hundred Fathoms Deep," Mr. T. Johnson ; pianofurte solo, Miss .Whittaker, R.A.M. (en- cored); song,"The Village Blacksmith,"Mr.Walter Shaw; song, "The Storm King," Mr. R. Johnson ; song, " Say Au Revoir," Mr. Wesley Cooke ; song, Mr. T. Johnson.; solo, Miss C. Taylor ; song, "The Better Land," Mrs. Temperley ; pianoforte solo, Miss Whittaker, R.A.M. Mr. Johnson (choirmaster) said he was requested by the officers and members of the choir, to tender to the good people who assisted them in the com- petition, their best thanks. Thes- (the civil acl,,ow. ledged their indebtedness, and were sure that if a like occasion came round again, they might denva I ,p on their services. He thought he !,oieht sly th. it all those who took part in the competition had been there that evening lee could have assured there that on behalf of the choir, they had their best thauks. There was another matter, and that was, that the best thanks of the meet- ing be given to the ladies and gentlemen who had gone to the trouble of decorating the room, and hld made it so nice, and also to the lady, who had given the piano- forte solos. He hoed that at the next social evening they would meet under the same circumstances as they had met that night. Mr. Brown seconded the vote of thanks which was carried unanimously. The balance sheet submit-md by the treasurer, Mrs. Wilton,showed the total receipts during the year to be £2l 18s. 9d., made up by the following items:—Balance in hand at the commencement of the year £lO 19s. 21; subscriptions and donations £8 ts. ; members' tees £2 181. 61. ; collection at lecture £1 10j. 91. ; per MISi Leathwood, fis. 4d. The Chairrnau said he was sure that no one would venture to say that woman was out of her proper sphere in carrying on that great Christian work. Woman lead a high place to fill and a high work to perform. Accord- ing to the appeintment of God she was man's com• panion, man's counsellor and man's comforter, and especially was her sphere within the sacred precinte of the home. It was given to woman ta sow the seeds,not for the immediate future, but for generations. As the home was the question fer her so NAAS the drink ques- tion, simply because it was the greatest enemy of home life and home joy. It was woman's question especially te fight the evil which had wrecked thousands upon thousands of homes. He believed that the women of England, especially those who loved Christ Jesus would not be doing their duty to their sisterg,husbands,brothera and their friends, if they had no such society as the British Women's Temperance Association. (Applause.) Mrs. Lea next addressed the meeting. In the course of her remarks she pleaded oe behalf of the child who was the sufferer through this great curse. Every child had a right to a home. (Hear, bear.) Alas ! the home had a rival, and many a child had been robbed of that blessing by the liquor traffic. N. enemy was so great as the eneiny of drunkenness. It was their duty to remove this great stumbling block. There were no two great institutions so antagonistic as the Church of Christ, and the liquor traffic. Children had a right to health and strength, and vigour, and how many did they find robbed of this right P They had a very serious duty to Perform in removing this great stumbling block out of the way of the children. Let them remove this drink from the grocer's shops, by deciding that they would not deal with one who held a licence. They wanted courage and perseverance. (Hear, hear.) Mrs. La then moved the following resolution :—" That title meeting views with satisfaction the great blessings that have accrued to Scotland,lreland,ani Wales,from the en- actment of Acts of Parliament, clesine licensed pretnises on the Lord's Day, and hereby affirms the princip'e of Imperial Sunday closing for the whole of the United Kingdom. (Applause.) Mr. Hardy seconded the resolution He said the United Kingdom Alliance was formed in 1853 It was not formed as a total abstinence society. They did not exact a pledge of total abstinence and yet it was a fact that the , power that had made up that organisation was the over. whelmine power of temperance men and wemen. He referred to Sunday closing in Scotland and spoke of the great success of the measure. They had no m.,re earnest and loyal supporters of Sunday closing in the House of Commons or out of it than the Scotch p-oole. They had now Sunday clesiee for Ireland. The meaeure had proved very beaeficial to that country. But,there were five cities that were at present exempted from the operation of the Act, and if Ireland was only master of her own situation she would soon bring these cities within the pale, and would present a much stronger argument in favonrof one day's prohibition out of seven than she did at present. Wales had also Ipen favoured with a similar measure, and it was only poor John Ball whe was lagging behind. He referred to workingmen who were crying out for eight hours a day, and yet they would have publicians working 15 hours a day and half a day en the Sabbath to gratify their thirst. In 1894 he visited Canada and stayed there seven months. He had seen more drunken- , ness in Liverpool in two hours than he saw during the whole of his seven mouths stay in Canada. He coa- t, ndcd it was the duty of the church to be in the fore- front of this temperance movement. Why should not the church have clean hands in regard to this business? Why should men and women be parties to this system of abomination of desolation ? He urged the members of the association to turn their face towards this foe and insist that it shall be overthrown, and God wonld be honoured and His name glorified by such a caurse. (Ap- plause)- The Rev. J. Osborne put the resolution to the meet' g and it was carried with acclamation. Votes of thanks to the Chairman and the speakers brought the meeting to a close. At intervals between the speeches several solos were sung by Mrs. A. Ellison Miss A. Cooke, and Miss B. Harrop.

The disturbance spread, and ultimately the mi'",ry were called out.

div.head: MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN.
div.p: MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN.
RUNCORN BRANCH.

The following is the annual report of Mr. W. Shaw. the reader-in-charge :—" The institute, the doors of which are thrown wide open to the sailors of every na- tioaality and of every creed, and also to the canal boat people who visit the port, has been a great bean. The , reading room is much more frequented. The weekly concerts and entertainments during the winter months have been well attended, and have been a refuge and counter-attraction to the temptations which Bur- ' round seamen during their time ashore. We specially thank our many friends who have given the concerts and lantern lectures. The Sunday evening services are well attended, ate] we have more masters of vessels and seaman attaindiug our services than we have had since the Runcorn branch was started. No doubt this is owing to the interest taken in them at Christmas time, to the visits paid to them on board their vessels in dock, and to help given at various times of reed, such as assisting some of them to the Liverpool hospitals, recevering bodies of thos) accidentally drowned, and burying them decently in the " sailors' grave." The Sunday school work is very encouraging. There is a marked change in the cleanliness and behaviour of the boat- men's children, and they come in large numbers. It would make this report too long were I to give the in- teresting cases which have some under my own notice during the past twelve months. I can only (with much thankfulness) mention the week of special service, the Watch Night service, the harvest thanksgiving services, the Jubilee, Whit Monday, and Christmas treats for sailors, the Sunday school treat, the annual excursion to Liverpool and New Brighton, and the ehildren's treat,up the river Weaver to Merbury Hall. All of these were successful except the excursion to Liverpool, which was marred by bad weather. The sailors and beat peo- ple have very warm friends in the Misses Hayes, of Frodeham,who supplied upwards of 200 woollen comfor- ters, helmets, mittens, Ito., for the Christmas gift to eel men, Ste., and during the summer sent us hunches of flowers every week to the institute. Mrs. Burton, At Proisham, very kindly presented the gifts on the sth January,assieted by the Misses Hayes. Mrs. C. 11.7.1 e burst sent a largo parcel of very useful articles for the beat children's Christmas tree. Several lady friends of the Mission have decided to make another effort to clear off the debt of £l5O which remains on the land. It has been decided to hold a sale of work in the institute on April 21st and 22nd, 1898, when it is hoped that the friends of sailors will I do their best to help this good work. In concluding my report, I wish to thank all my helpers who take part with me in giving the addresses at the services, the Sunday school teacbers,the choir,the organ. iet, those who keve helped at the weekly climates, and those who have given mill 'lsis Zse., and subscribed money for the treats at Cnristmas and Whitsuntide. Aurnincialt V. STocrroli Rum —This return match was played at Bowden on Saturday. The game was very fast throughout,and for some time neither side had the advantage. In the early part of the game the visi- tors made several determined rushes, and had bard luck owing to a good shot being saved directly under the cross-bar. Altrincham forwards now got away, and planted several goals in quick succession from the sticks of Davenport, Schwarz, and Frewer, bringing the score at half-time tl five goals to nil. In the second forty minutes the visitors' forwards combined better, and Kirkconnell, partly owing to his fleetness, got through the home defence and scored a beauty. •this caused Al- trincham to retaliate, and their forwards again ran the ball down and put in two more shots. A few minutes before the call of time Kirkconnell again got through from a pass on the left,and entering the circle alone took a deliberate shot at goal,but the homecustodian stopped the sh,*t with his body and cleared Go touch. The game ended in favour of Altrincham with a score of seven goals to one.

div.head: WARRINGTON DISTRICT NURSING • ASSOCIATION. CONCERT IN PARR HALL.,
div.p: WARRINGTON DISTRICT NURSING • ASSOCIATION. CONCERT IN PARR HALL.,

I Parr Hall was completely filled on Monday even- ing when the first concert was given in aid of the Warrington District Nursing Association, which is accomplishing such noble work among the poor of the town. The large attendance was chiefly due to 'the energetic action of those who had undertaken the onerous duties of ticket selling. Mr. E. Lloyd Jones acted as concert secretary to whom a meed of praise is due for the excellent arrangements which prevailed. Rarely has a concert been carried through with such alacrity and punctuality as characterised that on Monday night. In exactly two hours and a half no fewer than 34 items were given,ten of these being encores. The interval be- tween each item was of the briefest possible de- scription, and thus the continual waiting which tends to destroy the interest of the audienne at a concert was obviated. The leading artistes were Miss Mettle Mawdsley (soprano), Miss Juanita Jones (contralto), Mr. Harry Berrey (tenor), and Mr. James Rountree (bass). Miss ilettie Mawdsley was twice encored. She is gifted with a sweet soprano voice and her vocali- sation was characterised by artistic culture, clear enunciation, and a vivaciousness which captivated the audience. Her interpretation of "When the flowing tide comes in" and "Scenes that are bright- est" called forth a storm of applause and she was constrained to comply with encores. Her further contributions were "Dolly's Revenge" and "The nyder £:,e" which she sang with great success. Miss Juanita Jones' initial performance was" Father Eternal," but she did not develop her full powersl until later in the evening when she sang "Alone on the raft" and "Sweet Island of Ulva" in which her charming contralto voice was heard to advantage Both were sung with considerable taste and effec- tiveneas and she was encored on each occasion. Mr. Berrey used his pure toned tenor voice with credit- able effect. His three songs were ''Come into the garden liaud,"Tom Bowling,"and "The Holy City." In the last-named, the chorus was taken up by the Gitana Ladies Choir and considerably heigh- tened its effectiveness. Mr.Berrey sang in company with Miss Mawdsley in the duet"Anight in Venice." Mr. Rountree's best effort was " A hundred fathoms deep" which was sung with a dramatic expressicn and verve that secured him the demonstrative ap- proval of the audience. The chief honour of the evening, however, fell to the Birkenhead Gitana Ladies Choir, whose first appearance in Warrington was of such a flattering discription. Miss Maggie Davies wielded the baton and the music was given with a power and fi lish that was greatly appreci- ated. The light and shade were fully marked and the swing and balance of the parts were majestic in their precision. Six or seven choruses were given but the triumph of the evening was undoubtedly " Ash Grove" which was sung by special request. In response to the continued applause, the latter part was repeated. With regard to the instrumenta- lists the crown fell to Miss Jenny Parry who de- lighted the audience with several solos on the harp The harpist's contributions were " Morva Rhud- dlan " (Thonaas). " Autumn " (Thomas), " Within a mile of Edinboro "(Charles), and "The Keel Row" with variations. Her rendering of them was both brilliant and musicianly. She was encored. A similar compliment was paid the Gitana mandoline band consisting of five instrumentalists. They played three selections, all of which were given in a manner which was appreciated by the audience. The accompaniments during the evening were played with taste by Miss Maggie Davies and Miss Clara Waller. As a result of the concert neaily .£5O will be handed over to the funds of the institu- tion.

div.head: RUNCORN v. BRIGHOUSE RANUERS
div.p: RUNCORN v. BRIGHOUSE RANUERS
RE-PLAYED TIE.

A large gate assembled at Runcorn on Wednesday to see this re-played cup tie .Mr. Dillon,of Warrington,wds the referee and he had the following men under his , control. Runcorn : Houghton,full back; Warder,Butter- worth,Robinson and West, threequarter backs; Faulkner and Jolley, half backs; Langley,Walker,Moores,Farmer, Lightfoot, Gayter, Darlington and Bettley, forwards. Brighouse : Malay, fullback; Boothman,Brooke, Harder, Elolroyd, threequarter backs ; Ross and England, half backs; Wood,Nicholl, Croft,Armitage,Whiteley,Pullman, Priestley and Sugden, forwards. Brighouse won the toss and elected to play with the wind. Farmer started operations. Brighouse making a poor return. The homeaters were soon on the aggressive. Butterworth made desperate efforts to score and was just grassed under the goal post. Betley having mulled very badly Brighouse were almost let in, but Houghton got up in time and saved finely. The hornesters had now to use all ti.eir energy to keep their opponents back,as the latter were striving hard at the corner to be- come famous. A little later Butterworth was seen dish- ing along and passed all but he full back. Two of the Brighouse forwards came up behind and floored him. At this point the game was stopped Butter- worth being hurt. Be bad to leave the &gel and Gayer Got of the forwards filled his place. Play was ow very exciting and net without roughness A bout of passing initiated by Butterworth who had re- turned to the fir:d, and taken part in by Robinson and West, ended by the latter being knocked into touch near the line. After some give and take play the visitors commenced to rush, and carried the oval into very dan- gerous qoarters. Houghton saved grandly in the nick. ,of time by grounding the leather. Bunco n transferred matters to the opposite end, and Brighouse were pena- lised but nothing came of the homesters kick. Half- time arrived with a clean sheet. Soon after the restart Faulkner got the ball from a scrimmage, and passed to Butterworth the latter placing the oval over the line in fine style,and amid a loud outburst of applause from the Cleehire and Lancashire supporters. A good attempt at goal was made by Jolley, For obstruction at centre the home team were awarded a free kick. Jolley afterwerde started a round of passing and play was carried to the visitors half by Butterworth, The latter parted with the leather very slowly and Brighouse stayed progress. Houghton came on the scene and tackled brilliantly. Butterworth punted the ball from the goal posts the oval just falling a few inches short of going over. tint. terworth cut the work fine for the backs by securing the tall. He made a dash for the line and when on the point of being floored be sent to Warder. The latter re- passed, and Butterworth scored a second try, joiloc kicking the goal from an easy place. Jolley afterwards got possession, and passing to Butterworth the latter ran over again and placed the leather in • safe position. The goal kick was taken by Jolley. but nothing came of it. The visitors appeared to be quite over-powered and could hardly keep the Cestriana out of their quarters. They commenced the kick and rush game, but this did not come off as Runcorn were pre- pared for it. The latter got away and matters were seen in their opponents 25. Rugden was severely admonished by Mr. Dillon for his conduct. Brighouee emerged from their dangerous position and the sport was being eagerly played in the Cestrians' quarters. Every effort was made by them to score as s son as they secured the leather,one or more of the hememen pounced upon them. The Yorkshiremen were penalised for off-side play, and a free kick granted to Runcorn brought the desired re- lief. The game now became very exciting the visitors striving with all their might to sm... The game shortly afterwards ended with Runcorn bein,z winners by ors,. goal, three tries, (11 points) to Brighouse nil.

div.head: TEIE CONDITION OF THESSAIy. MR. T. W. LEGH'S REPORT.
div.p: TEIE CONDITION OF THESSAIy. MR. T. W. LEGH'S REPORT.

The Athens correspondent of the " Times" writes : Mr. T. W. Legh. M.P., who, .actiag on behalf of the Duke of Westminster's Dammittee,has travelled through all the distrilts of Thessaly, has arrived here. He de- scribes the state of the country V on the whole better than might have been expected. The principal devasta- tion took place in the localities traversed by the Turkish army. Most of the damage was done either by Turkish irregulars or tic 4ishanded Greek ‘''"4",nt^Prs and pri Boners released from Larissa gaol. Karaklar and Velis- tino eapeciany miff r.e,l severely. On the other hand, Kalambaka,Trikhata,and other to-vris escaped all injury The agricultural population remains on the whole unmo. lested,though compdled to submit to taxation. The right to levy taxes is claimed by the Turka,on the :ground that the country is not only occupied but administered by Turkey. In the isolated cases of pillage and extortion the offenders are inferior officers commanding small de- tachments. The general conduct of the Turkish troops is excellent. An earnest desire is expressed by both efficere and men that evacuation shall take place as speedily as possible. The Redifs especially are anxious to return home, as the season of the spring sowing is at hand. It is feared, however, that owing to the prema- ture proposal of Prince George's camiidature the Sultan will find excuses for prolonging the occupation. The menacing attitude of Bulgaria also causes serious mis- givings to the army, neither officers nor men relishing the prospect of another campaign. The army of occu- pation numbers 80,000 men.

RUGBY FOOTBALL.

There could be ho mistaking the fact that Saturday'e match was a " friendly" encounter. The attendance would hardly do credit to an "A " team match and there was little or no entlausianz amongst either players or spectators. Even the flag thas floats over one of the stands fluttered so lazily and intermittently as to sug- gest that it didn't care one bit about the combat taking place underneath, and seemed almost half-ashamed of the letters" W.F.C." emblazoned upon it. The rumpurs that Leeds were to visit the Wilderspool enclosure gave place to St. Helens later on ha the week,and for the third time this season the wearers of the blue and white stripes I faced those with primrose and blue, which, bye the bye. have almost given place to another colour entirely ou many of the jerseys, The two teams may be regarded as brothers in adversity for both received the knock out in the first round of the cup ties on the previous Satur- day. Sr. Helens may be said to have received the heaviest knock of the two, but despite their downfall, ' both came up smiling on Saturday as if nothing had happened.

The match was a most interesting one ; in fact it was far better than many anticipated. In the two previous encounters this season Warrington had come off victori- ous,and there seemed no grounds for thinking that they would be unable to do the trick again. St. Heins are not what a football club's treasurer would term a draw- ing team,or in other words, a go)d lever for diverting cash from the pockets cf individuals into a club's trea- sury. It is questionable whether half-a-dozm St.Helens people entered the Wilderspool enclosure as spectators, and as little interest was taken in the engagement at Warrington,Saturday's receipts must have fallni almost to zro. When the teams entered the field it was seen thar, they were fairly reprnentative. Bate', place at half back was taken by his brother, R. Bate, who, from hll appearances is a player of promise. Heesom was un- able to occupy his accustomed position in the three- quarter line, and Cross stepped into the breach.

Ideal football weather prevailed, and for the first half Warrington had the assistance of a gentle breez at their hacks. From the outset it was seen that the Sr. Helens men were determined, if possib:e, to retrieve their previ- ous defeats For the first quarter of an hour the Wat- rington men were kept bush) „Mending, and they were fortunate to escape with not rig more substarati Limn a dropped goal registered ag,:.i,lst them. The hem, team at length roused itself to a .upronae effo.t, and remark- able as it may reem,they were eaccesAul on the oucauio,i of their first invasion. 1.3.4te put the finhhing tor.ce to a fine concerted effort between tire threequarters and half backs, and therefore may b;, c moldered to have reached the height of his ambition by scoring in his initial Ina eo in first-class football. As goal-kicking is not a point with Warrington, it wag not at all surnrism ti .t the additional points were not ti-cured. Very K., irt'i• after this another try was registered for the home team, and this was undoubtedly due to a fine effort by Moores, although Naylor planted the ball over the line. Alter a tricky movement, Moores centred the ball beautifully, and Naylor at one bound crossed the line. There was again another attempt to kick a goal, but, of course, the ball went awry of the goal posts. This completed the work of the gentleman in charge of the scoring board, and although the second half was unproductive of tries and goals, the interest in the match was maintained until the close.

To speak of the individual players, the first and fore- most place must be given to Traynor, who, although on the losing side was a continual blister to big opponents. He is certainly a player who deserves a high poaition amongst first-class footballers. He possesses speed, stamina, and unlimited resource, which servo him well when his team are in dfficulties. Whiteley was the best of the visiting half-backs, and his dropned goal was a meritorious effort. The two f ull-baeks —Foulkes and oscow—were well matched, although the latter's play seems to be deteriorating of late. Both Moores and Isherwood played a brilliant game on the Warrington side, and altogether the threequarter line seemed stronger than for some time past. Hallam plays a far better game on the wing than in the centre, and be now seems to have got into the right position. Cross captained the team with his usual ability,but as a player he ia far different from the Cross of twelve months ago. R.Bate may be said to have made a very favourable impression on making his debut in first-class football. Hi a lightness tells against him when pitted against a burly opponent, but beyond that he is both active and resourceful.and although not to be compared with " Smack," be may still become a credit- able half back to partner his more distinguished brother. In the forward ranks Warrineton had slightly the advan- tage. although it was some time before the backs took advantage of the forwards heeling out from the scrim- mages.

Not thst Yorkshire clubs are in any means dobe within the compt,tition,hut the vicrories gained by clubs in the br,srd-aered shire were mtinlv against second-class team., and were not to bo com- pared as real trials of strength with tht ties already alluded to.

Widnes are a particularly hard nut to crack, and may yet enter the final. Saturday's match was a tremend- ously hard struggle, and the issue was in doubt right to the cloie, but the '6 Chemicals " nisnatd to come out on top by a single point, though th-ir ijnwis. cacti.... to- wards the close mighteasily have changed a victory into defeat. Equally keen was the struggle at Broughton, where the iarnous old cup fighters in Wakefield Trinity bit the dust. The tackling on both sides was particularly effective, and only by a solitary try to nothing dui the Raeg,ers manage to enter round number three. Probably the most meritorious performance in the lot was the victory of Oldham at Halifax, and it is quite evident that in additims to their ambition to win the Lancashire championship, Oldham have very serious designs upon the Cup trophy.

The Lancashire Second Division clubs can scarcely be said to have covered thenvelVes with glory in the cup ties, but mire than one of them came out of their trying ordeals with distinct credit. Barr )w gave an unclre. monlv Smut clniplay at Huddersfield, Radcliffe struggled garnet : under the huge difficulties at HO, whilst Walk- den, who had been persuaded to visit Batley for the whole of :Ise gate less :Waal expenses, were not over- vrlie!med by anything like the score anticipated. --- A ereat deal of interest centred in the doings of the two Cheshire clubs, Runcorn and Birkenhead Wanderers. Both einemlarly enough were pitted against strong York- shire clubs, and both came out with distinct credit. Almost up to the CTOSf3 of play, indeed Runcorn had won their match at Brighouse, but though they fully deserved to do au on the elae's play they had te be content with a draw, whilst the Wanderers were somewhat unlucky in suffering defeat at the hands of Bradford, who were un- able to score until late on in the game. Of the York- shire clubs visiting Lancashire only Bramley returned victorious, and this by a aolitary print over Rochdale Hornets, who in the first round had somewhat easily defeated Holbeck. Salford and Leioh were hoth en- gaoed in mere farces, and the huce scores obtained are sufficient indication of the absurdity of clubs like Abbey Hill and Lees ever getting so far as the second round, !

The draw for the third round,which, by the way, will not be played until the 1912 inst., provides several particularly interesting matches. Bradford will have a pretty stiff task at Hull, as will Tluddersfield to come out victorious against Broughton Rangers. Fleetwood are pretty safe to say good-bye to the Cup, seeing they entertained the " dark horse " of the competition in the Hull Kingston Rovers and whom Warrington have cause ,to remember. Barnton can scarcely be expected to sue- need where Rochdale Hornets failed. Salford have another easy journey, against Altrinchara, to wit, but Leigh v. Last year's winners go to Castleford, and, barring accidents, should land in the fourth round, especially judging by Castle. ford's somewhat defundory display against a team like Whitworth.

Everybody appeared conscioua of same approaching event early in the afternoon, and. an encoirer would have learned that a cap-tie match with Hunslnt was down for 3.30. The match itself was a thor.ugh cup tie battle, and after a foul charge by the Hunslet tront rank early on, there wasiwas no kil-gloved handling of an opponent. After Bitey's fine goal, the re- doub:able Albert Goldthorpe •broke his own record, made the score even,and pleas.zd all impartial spectat Ha, by a beautiful dropkick which sent the ball over. In the second half lilunsl,,t gave Widnes a warm time, and put on flee more points with the aid of a grand try by Hannah, and a placed gual tram the deadly toe of "Al- bert." To the last minute Ulu issue was in doubt, and the struggle was of the most delightfully keen nature. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A SERIOUS OUTCOME_ OF STONE TRROWING--4. WOMAN
NEARLY KILLED.

On Monday morning at the Warrington Borough Police Court before M. F. Monks (in the chair), Mr. T. Birchall, Mr. S. Wright. Councillor J. Shaw Green, al d Cnincillor Smethursz, John Robinson (11), 15, Greenall Street, was charged with throwing stones In Church- street, on the 21st Fehruary.—The Chief Constable said that this was an exceptional case, On the day in ques- tion a poor old woman, a hawker of lemons and oranges named Bridget Macdermott was about to enter the " Little Wonder," in Chernh street. She had a box on her shculder. The defendant said to some other chil- dren who were tormenting her, as was usual with them, "Seems hit the box she is carrying." She happened .o turn round at the time, and was struck by the stone in tße forehead, causing her to fall to the ground in an un- conscious condition. She was at once taken to the In- firmary, and for a time her life was in danger. It was not known at the time who had thrown the stone. He had summoned the lad, not for the assault, but for throwing the stnne. The windows in the poor womaa's house were broken by lads who were in the habit of throwing stones at them. The defendant was one of the ringleaders. When inquiriers were first made this lad volunteered the statement that it was a girl who had thrown the stone, but the police afterwards found it was himself.—At this point the complainant was called before the bench and appeared ill and weak. She remarked that she hal only done a bit of work, and but for the ladies and gentlemen of Warrington she would have starved.—The boy's father said he had been in bad company for the last three months and had sometimes stayed out all night.—The Chief Constable suggested that three days' detention in the police celle would do the lad good.— Mr, Monks: I don't think that would be as effective as birching.—The Clerk explained that the bench had no power to order the lad to he birched. (To the father) : Will you birch the lad here ?—The Father: No ; I should not like to do so.—Mr. Birehall wonder your son is incorrigible —Mr. Monks "Spare the rod and spoil the child."—lt was eventually decided that the defendant should be kept in the cells three days,and at the Chief Constable's suggestion, that the old womsn be allowed ss. out of the n 'or box.

div.head: FRIENDLY ENCOUNTER AT HOME
div.p: A FRIENDLY ENCOUNTER AT HOME
ST. HELENS AGAIN BEATEN.
Th.,re was but a mall attendance on the Wilder-

spool enclosure on Suturday afternoon when War- rington and St. Helens played for the third time this season. The match was of course a "friendly," the enceunter having been arranged after the knock-out in the cup ties of the previous week. The weather was ideal for football, and an interest- ing game was witnessed. Pepresentative teams entered the field. In the Warrington fifteen, R. Bate entered the lists in place of his brother, and Heesom's position in the three-quarter line was filled by Cross,who captained the team. The teams were as follows : _
_ Warrington: Boscow, back ; Nloores, Isherwood, Cross and Hallam, three-quarters; R. Bate and Duckworth, half-backs; Taylor, Naylor, Deakin, Morrison, Swift, Mason, Barrett, and Fairhurst, forwards.

St. Helena : Foulkes, back; Morrison, Doherty, Traycor, and Rutter, three-quarters ; " Green " and Whiteley, half-backs ; Dale, Winstanley, Caveney, Thompson, Gladwin, Sudlow, Briers, and R. Taylor, forwards. Winning the toss, the home team played with the slight breeze at their backs in the first half. Traynor started operations, and Isnerwood resir:nded with in- terest. The home forwards placed Warrington on the aggressive, but Traynor WAS early prominent with a smart run and kick. By quick following up, the St. Helens forwards reached time home twenty-five, and al- though Moores eased the pressure slightly, the ball was carried near to the home goal line. A scrimmage en- sued,,nd Whiteley getting possession dropped a splendid goal within a few minutes from the start. From the restart the visitors again asserted themselves, Traynor being again conspicuous in the attack. Caveney made his mark, and St. Helens were again hovering in close proximity to the home line. A rush by the Warrington forwards relieved the pressure, and Moores getting pos- session gave trouble. Foulkes was called upon to defend, and cleared out his opponents in fine style. The St. Helens forwards were again prominent, and Briers ex- perienced hard lines in being he don the line. It was not until atter the first quarter of an hour had elapsed that the Warrington men gained any substantial footing in the St. Helena quarters, and then they scored. The forwards by combining well gave the backs an oppor- tunity to shine. A fine passime movement between Cross, ' Duckworth, Isherwood, and R. Bate resulted in the lit- ' ter crossing the coveted line. faallam took the place kick, and had hard lines in not kicking a goal. Encouraged by this success the Warrington men con- tinued to play a fine game. Hallam was noticeable for a short run and kick into tne open, which he followed up cleverly by putting his men on side. Traynor did his utmost to keep the Warrington men at bay, but a moment later Moores made a dodgy run through his opponents ranks, and by a dedicious kick into the goal mouth, Naylor bounded over the line in irresistible fashion. Ttie goal kick was again a failure. Just be- fore the interval Traynor neatly intercepted a pass, but was knocked into touch by Boscow when nearing the line. At half-time the score stood, Warrington two tries (six points), to St.Helens nrie goal (two points.) Early in the second half Foulkes was called upon to touch doan as the result of a passing movement, and a kick by Meores. Isherwood WAS prominent by a smart ran,bist Foulkes'proved the stumbling block. Tall kick- ing gave the vieitons an advantage, and hot work was witnessed under the home poste. Green made • bold attempt to score, but the tackling was very line. pair_ burst steered, and Warrington again attacked, Traynor once raore rendering yeoman service to the visitors. During the last stage the pace Mac armed somewhat, and St. Helens looked dangerous until Moores cleared. Twice Warrington saved. Capital passing by the home quarter line was checked by DMerty, but another bout saw the St. Helens goal threatened. Warrington attacked atrongly, and Hallam Was prominent with a sterlieg kick, which was not taken advantage of. Isher- wood next ran firoly,but all efforts had a futile ending. The score at the close of play therefore remained un- altered, Warrington winning by all points to two.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CITURCIIES. --- WYCLIFFE P.S.A. ANNIVERSARY.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CITURCIIES. --- WYCLIFFE P.S.A. ANNIVERSARY.

There was a large attendanca at toe anniversary of the Y.S.A. Society held at Wychffs Church on Sunday afternoon. The Rev. J: Yong 4 presided, and in the course of a few remarks expressed an earnest hops that they would make the P.S.A. Society still more success- ful this year than i had been in th past.—Dr. Waite, of Liverpool. delivered a short address, in which be con- trasted Christianity with Socialism,contending that both could not run together. The difference between Chris- tianity and Socialism was that Christianity strove to im- prove-the man whilst Socialism aimed at improving a man's circuin itances without any direct or special effort to improve the man himr.elf. The Socialist's contention was that if the circumstances of a msn were improved he would become better, while Christianity held that the only way to improve a man's circumstances was to beg n by improving the man himself. Happiness, he pointed out,did not depend upon circumstances, but upon char- acter. Dr. Waite an 1 Mr. W. H. Waite, his con, sang a duet,entitled "It is pleasant to sing." Mr. W. El. Waite also samr " Zion " and recited " A City Tale." The Rev. J. Yonge announced that the number of members on the register during the previous year was 903, which was not quite up to the membership f tho previous 12 : months,but still ie was satisfactory,and they hoped to do better this year. That day 542 had enrolled. Mr. Farrar read the devotional ezercisee,aud Mr. W. H. Waite read the Scripture l'sson. A collection was taken on behalf ,of the renovation funds.

WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL. THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS ELECTION.

There was a ineetiag of the Warrington Trades and !About Council on Tuesday evening at the Waggon and Horses Hotel, Buttermarket-street. In the absence of the President, the chair was occupied by Mr. A. Lang. Thera was a good attendance of delegates.

THE ELECTION OF GUARDIANS. A letter was read from Alderman Sutten on behalf of the Conservative Association stating that the Association had decided not to offer any opposition to the candidates brought out by the Council for seats on the Board of Guardians—Mr. T. B. Malkin and Mr. J. Batteraby,and that they considered it was desirable in the interests of the borough that a contested election of Guardians should, if possible, be avoided.—The Secretary (Mr. Bul- lock) inforrned the Council that he bad received no re- ply from the Liberal Association in answer to his com- munication.

The Climaxes( said the delegates would no doub be aware of the step the Council took at the last meeting. They had two nominations for St. John's Ward, but Mr. Malkin,they expected,would be returned unopposed unless some independent man came out and tried to oust him. It was necessary that they should take some definite step, in the matter. Mr. Elms asked whether it was of any importance to have members on the Board of Guardians ?

The SBCRETARY (Mr. Bullock) considered that it was not worth while having a contested election for a guar- dian, and as a communication had not yet been received from the Liberal Association, they did not know whether they would be opposed or net. Mr. PODMORB said they decided at the last meeting to bold the two wards they possessed, and be took it that they then decided to undertake all responsibility. The CHAIRMAN said they did not gain anything directly by having representatives on public bodies, but they benefited indirectly. There were many matters which came before the Board of Guardians which were dealt with by people who had not a full knowledge of the con- ditions under which poor people lived. On many occa- sions, especially on relief committees, working men had a great influence in Jealing with cases that came 'before them. Mr. SAMBROOK thought it was necessary that they soould have some practical working men on the Board of Guardians. Mr. Poi:intone asked whether the delegates bad re- ceived any instructions from their branches as ta how they should vote with reference to the two candidates suggested by the Council for St. John's Ward. His. branch had instructed him which man to vote for. The CHAIRMAN said there were no instructions given to the delegates to ascertain the feeling of the branches with reference to the two men brought forward. Mr. S. WRIGHT remarked th3t tbey must fight the election as a united council, and not allow any political bias to influence them.

Mr. BATTERSEY in referring to the political views he held, said he was more Liberal on trades union matters than those who professed to be Liberals. Voting by ballot then took place to select a candidate for St. John's Ward. The members submitted were Mr. Battersby and Mr. Delaney. S von voted for Mr. Bat- tersby and six for Mr. Delaney, and the former was adopted as the Council's candidate.—Mr. Battersby thanked the members for selecting him as their candi- date.
an election committee wam afterwards formed. SUGGESTED PEDERLTION OF _TRADES COUNCILS.

A communication was received from the Manchester and Salford Trades and Labour Council stating that the quosion of federation was at the present time deeply engaging the attention of all trade unionistS, and the members of the Manchester and Salford Trades and Labour Council had had under consideration the advisa- bility of eadeaysuring te bring about a federation of trades councils of the whole of Ltncashire,they being of opinion that by a federation of this character much good might be achieved and workers in different towns and cih in the county brought into closer touch and sym- pathy with each other on all questions industrial and social. It would also be a means of developing greater concentration of energy and thought, which if accom- panied by simultaneous action on the part of the visrious councils on any question affecting the interests or the workers would be found of great advantage. Numerous instances might be quoted of the value of this sug,gested combination which would be better and easier to discuss in confidence than to attempt to set forth in detail in a circular. The Warrington Council was asked to consent to he represented at a meeting to be convened by the Manchester and Salford Council and held in Manchester, for the purpoee of discussing and if agreed upon, after being referred to the respective counclia,to form a feth.t. ation of Trades Councils of Laricashire.—lt was decided tO arip)int Mr. Binke as a delegate of the Warrington Council to the Conference. Played at Widnes More about 6000. Johnson set the oval rolling. Immediately a serimmsee ensued on the • half-way line, and Widnes were peneezed„ Peters after- wards making his mark. Frem here the ball landed in touch, and the visitors' left wing "got goine" but their course was barred at midway, "Butcher " Rispan gain- ing ground by a punt. Mitchell, the visitors' back, re- ceived, and punted well up the field, tackling Batey before he could reepond. A ecere loeked imminent,when Brennan saved grandly. Widnes played on the aggres- slue, and reached the Hunslet territory, but a splendid passing movement between Murthy,Douglas,Nevitt, Ris- pan, and Brennan was mulled by a foreword throw. Batey obtained possession, and punted up the field. Hampson received, but a sure try was missed by forward play. Rushing up Batey dropped a magnificent goal from near midway. Resuming, Widnes were awarded a free kick for fore factics on the part of the visitors. Play near the half- way line, saw Albert Goldthorpe obtain possession, and running up the Widnes goal looked in danger of being taken, when Nevitt tackled grandly. Hunslet were awarded a free kick from the serial:Page, but A. Gold- thorpe failed to augment the score. A pretty passing movement on the part of the visitors almost culminated in something tangible, but a forward pass spoiled the venue. Widnes were penalized whilst the game was h^leg contested in der gerous proximity to their goal, but nothing accrued. Considerable ground was gained from a punt by Batey, hut tnis was nullified as the re- sult of passing on the part of the visitors. Not to be repulsed in such an easy manner, Widnes returned, and Murphy initiated some pretty parsing,Leyshon which resulted g beiug held up on the line amid tremendous excitement. Rispan essayed at goal, but the ball shved the bar On in resumption both teams were repeatedly penalized. 1 u nothin worthy of a note, resulted. The visitors pressed into the home half. where Albert Goldthorpe equalized the score by dropping pretty goal amid the wild cheers of the }lnnate contingent. Widnes went away in a most Irresistible manner from the restart, tint the visitors were allowed a mark, the fiunslat " goal kicker " failing miserably to negoeiate. After some rather desultory Play in the visitors' territory, the spectators were again treated tea splendid piece of work in the shape of a try by Grace. This player printed rip the field, and before the leather could bc returned he charged the kick down, and dribbing up scored amid a thunder of ap- plause. Hatay failed at tile goal kielc• Play had hardly been going on five minutes, when Leyshon charged down a return kick,aed placed behind the poets which seemed to dog B stey all throu2h the thus adding the second try for Widn The ill-luck es. game when attempting to convert tries FiVin manifested itself, and the score was not increased. Tire half-time score was as 'goal. Subsequent to the cuatornary"breather" all et f°llewa:—Widnes, nem goal two tiles : Eiunslet, one re-commenceu operations, Nevitt returning, but a deal of dry play was imparted to th game to a super- fluity of exchange kicking. Tire visitors rushed a Scrim- mage,e owing and a scare seemed inevitable when Novitt exe- cuted a daring save. Reciting play ensued, in which both teams hail a fair share of the argument, isut at length Peters was forced to concede a dead ball. Imme- diately on resumption' the visited; were back again,and numerous grand eaves were effected by the home team. At a later stage of the proceedings Hannah succeeded in adding to the visitor,' (mole, by a eplinodid try, A. Geld- thorpe landings goal. When the final arrived the score was—Widnes, eight pointr; Hunslet, seven points.

div.p: THE Ray. J. B. THURSTON.

The Rev. J. B. Thurston .pi:e-aaW:cl—;;i,i farewell sermon at the Parish Church on Sunday morniu, and at St. George's Mission in the V ening.The latter edifice was crowded. The rev. gentleman will be inducted to the Lymm living this afternoon, and it is expected there will be a large number of friends present from Warrington. LODGE M ERTING. GOOD TEMPLAMY.—DISTRICT

he annual session of the District Lodge of South West Lancashire was held at Wesley Hall, Liverpool, on Saturday. Rev. J. A. Lee, D.C.T..pre- , sided. Representatives were present from Liverpool, Southport, Earlestown,Asliton-in-Makerfield,Leigh, St.Helens,Warrington,Widnes,Wigan, and Tyldesley and also several visitors from West Cheshire District and Manchester. The district degree was conferred on 31 candidates, after which the officers' reports were given, The D.C.T. reported on the healthy condition of the order,and urged them on to greater I activity in their work. He spoke of the soccess of the bazaar recently held in Liverpool, and of new lodges being instituted, the No. 1 Convention piny- ing a prominent part in the success of the same. The D. Secretary reported an increase of 146 in 47 lodges. The D. Treasurer reported a good balance in hand. The D.E.Superintendent reported on work done in the district. The D.S.J.T.reported on work done among the juveniles. All the reports were adopted, and the election of offieers for the coming year took place, the following being elected : D.C.T. J. A. div.head: ALLEGED WRONGFUL DISMISSAL.
div.p: ALLEGED WRONGFUL DISMISSAL.

Before His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes,at the War- rington County Court on Thursday,last week, an action was heard in which Henry Jackson,of Wellington-street, Warrington, claimed £3 125., from the Cheshire Lines Committee for alleged wrongful dismissal. Mr. T Swift of Liverpool (instructed by Messrs. Swift, Garner and Company) appeared for the plaintiff, and ,Mr. Jordan, of Manchester, (instructed by Messrs. Lingard,Manches- ter) represented the defendants. In opening the case Mr. Swift stated that at the end of October, or the beginning of the following month, the plaintiff was su-pended for a week, arid it came about in this way. The plaintiff was employed as an excava- tor and was sometimes expected to work overtime, sometimes commencin4 at midnight on Saturday. On the 30th of October when the plaintiff finished his week's work he was asked to recommence work at midnight. He did so and worked continuously for 28 hours more. The consequence was that he con- tracted a severe cold. On the following Friday the plain- tiff was too unwell to work and told the foreman. He lleft his work and intended if he were well enough to ' start work at midnight on Saturday. He, however, failed to get up at the proper time, and did not arrive , until nearly four o'clock on Sunday morning. He found I that he was in plenty of time but he was told that his I check had been turned. On the following morning the plaintiff saw the foreman wbo told him to see the In 1 Spector again on the following Monday. This was the week's suspension alluded to. He did so and was in- formed that he was not to start because there was a letter from the headquarters stating that he was not to be taken on again. He was denied work and was not given notice. It was the custom to give 14 days notice. Mr. Swift proceeded to read the correspondence which had taken place on the subject, in which Mr. Meldrum the manager of the Cheshire Lines Committee, stated that the plaintiff was discharged for general inattention and disobedience to orders. He denied that the Company were liable for any damages for dismissing Jackson.

Henry Jackson, the plaintiff, stated that be entered the Cheshire Lines Committee's employ 73/4 years ago. They received pay at the rate ot time and a half for Sunday work. On Sunday,October 30 and following day be was practically at work for 29 hours at one stretch. In consequence of the exposure he received a severe cold. He worked on the following Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday, and on the Friday be complaihed to William Wright of feeling ill. The foreman asked him whether he would be able to commence work at mid- I night on Saturday again, and witness replied Mat he would turn out if he possibly could. Witness intended to arrive at twelve o'clock, but overslept himself and did not arrive until nearly four o'clock. On arrival he was told that "his check bad been turned" and that another man had been started in his place. Cross-examined by Mr. Jordan : He had not seen the book of rules, nor had be signed the leaflet produced. It was not his signature. He had not seen the rule which stated that any man who absented himself from duty without leave was liable to instant dismissal. He bad asked for a cspy of the rules but hae never received it. On Saturday after- noon, the 6th November, the night on which he was to start work, he admitted that be was in the Cross Keys in company with another man, and that Mrs. Anderton trsfused to serve them. It was on account of the condi- tion of the other man. Ile only had three half-pints of beer. Richard Tickle, 24, Dudley-street, Warrington, stated that be was a s!ater. He was in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Committee, and when the men were wanted for night work their names were posted on the shop door. The men did not turn up if they did not want. (Laughter.) When a man did not turn up he was asked by tne Inspector the reason, and if he gave a reasonable explanation it was satisfactory. He had never known a man discharged for not going to work on Sunday. _ . . .

George-Rowe, 59, Oliver-streec, Warrington, said he had omitted to go to his work on the Cheshire Lines Railway on Sundays. He was suspended for a day on one occasion for doing so.—Cross-examined : Ho con- sidered that the men were treated severely for little offences.

Jostph William Allen, gas engineer, said the plaintiff called at his house, 36, Wellington-street, on Saturday evening, about 9.30, on November 6th, and he was then perfectly sober.—Cross-examined: Someone had told him that plaintiff bad been charged with drunkenness. Bridget Jackson, wife of the plaintiff, also gave evi- dence. This conc:uded the case for the plaintiff. Mr. Jordan asked His Honour whether he was satisfied that there was a case to answer. His Honour replied that he thought there was, and that the defendant's witnesses should be called. The case was then adjourned until the next court on March 17th.

This week's Australian wail contains accounts of the great heat in the colonies. Captain Sturt, the explorer, relates how once, somewhere in the great Australian Desert, the mercury in his thermometer, which was graduated up to 127 deg., burst the bulb. During the recent heat waves the thermometers in many localities registered in the open sun over 160 deg., and the shade registers are even more expressive. On December 30, under severe shade conditions, 107•3 deg. was registered at the Melbourne Observatory' and on January'll a still higher record, 109.5 deg., was reached. At Boort (Vic- toria) the shade register was 116 deg.; at Oraeo, perched high in the snowy and wind-blown Alps, the record was 105 deg. in the shade.

Dining cars are excellent institutions, but even the model ones on the Great Northern are not adapted for outside passengers. Mr. Faber, the Danish Consul as Newcastle, tried the experiment on Saturday. Leaving at King's-cross by the quarter to six, it occurred to him to change into the dining car at Finsbury-park. The train began to move before he could jet on board. He mounted the step and tried a door only to find it fastened, He thumped at door and window, but nobody hearing him, the luckless passenger had to hold on tight and make up his mind to be rattied along at express Speed for more than seventy miles. He found it very cold and dirty travelling, but he held tight till eighteen minutes past seven, when Peterborough was reached. Then Mr. Faber had a wash and got his dinner. Moral for travellers : Don't change carriages at Finsbury- park.

The heavy fall in both the import and export returns of the past month, as shown by the Board of Trade re- turns for the past two months, is a matter for serious consideration. The falling off in the imports, which amounts to £1,474,290, is mainly due to a reduction in the quantities of raw materials for our various manu- factures. Chief among these are the reduced entries of metals, chemicals, wool, and the supplies for genera manufactures. Raw cotton has increased in quantity but declined considerably in estimated value. Taking the two months of the present year together, the reduc- tion represents an estimated value of £1,320,627, The fall in exports for both periods is also entirely the result of the limited shipments of machinery and mill work. Metals and apparel show also a reduced demand. The city of Chicago has long had a reputation for cos- mopolitanism not even second to that of New York. Chief Justice Fuller is said to have declared that it con- tained"more Poles than any city in Poland,more Bohem- ians than any city in Bohemia, more Germans than in any city in Germany save Berlin, more Irish than any city in Ireland save Dublin, more Italians than any city in Italy save Naples and Rome," and now Associate Justice Brewer has capped this by adding that it has "doubtless more saints and sinners than any places save heaven and bell." The latter judge also declares that, thanks to the Chicago Divorce Courts, "a Chicago man may have even a thousand wives,like holomon in all his glory,provided he will take them consecutively and not contemporaneously."

div.p: *, Warrington, 4th March, 189 i.
"THE CHIEF CONSTABLE AND THE IRISH.

- _ MEN OF WARRINGTON." Sir,—ln reading my " Examiner "on Saturday last I was very glad to find our Chief Constable's explanation of his observations in reference to ths Wf at of Ireland labourers, on the 4th nit, His apology however, is a tame one, to the public in general, and the ten thousand Irish people who reside in Warrington, in particular. He says his expresfion was "that the West of Ireland labourers were a blood thirsty lot when in drink," which bad appeared in some of the newspapers minus the word " when in drink." In one sentence he gives us sugar, and in the next stick. May I respectfully point out to the Chief Constable, that every prisoner is tried by English law, on his, sr her own responsibility, and that conviction or acquittal as the case may be is the result. Why then, should aspersions, I cast in the teeth of that nationality to which the prisoner may be of? Mr. Talbot, is a public man, than whom I hold ne one in higher estimation, tut, as such, he, as well as others must be criticised even adversely, whereever and whenf ever their zeal carries them away against any section o the community, In exaggeration. Now, sir, whether in drink or not I absolutely deny the accuracy of that statement. On the contrary the West of Ireland labourers are the most peaceful and sober class in the thiel kingdoms By what logic or process of reasoning dc,.e he c in to such a conclusion? As well might we contend that because s certain lord— whose name I will not mention lest I might hurt the susceptibilities of any of his friends—committed forgery recently; for which he is now an inmate of Wormwood Scrub, for a term of five years, that every lord in the land, every member of the House of Lords, the lords spiritual, as well as the lords temporal, are forgers, or that, because of the atrocity of Deeming, at Rainhill, every Englishman in that district must be atrocious.— Yours truly,

div.head: SHEMIS PHAIIRICK.
div.p: SHEMIS PHAIIRICK.

THE RECENT DEBATES ON SPIRITUALISM. Sir,—l hope I need offer no apology for taking up a little of the " Examiner's" space with a few words anent the recent debates. Thought moves along very definite lines. Yesterday it was the infidel versus the Christian, to-day it is the Spiritualistic Christian who takes up arms against his brother Christian minus all Spiritualism. What it may be to-morrow we need not trouble ourselves to think of, always feeling an inward satisfaction with humanity's gain from unbelief. It is net with the debate proper that I wish to deal, but with a few of the words that fell from the lips of my old Need, Councillor F. It. Roberts, and I hope he will not take them amiss. Mr. Roberts told his audience that ' Secularism was a form of unbelief, which had had considerable vogue, but was now receding from men's minds. Tricked out in a certain show of knowledge,and hiding under the names of certain physical scientists who seemed to have laid bare the foundations of the universe, it had captured minds incapable of much thought,but capable of hero worship." Possibly Mr. Roberts knows all about secularism, and this being so he ought to have told his audience that Mr. Holyeake, the author of the term, maintained that secu- larism does not involve scepticism, that it was a new form of free thought, perfectly independent of Atheism or Theism. But this is a small matter. I prefer to take Mr. Bradlaugh's definition of the term as given in his debate with Dr. McCann. "I think," he avowed," that the consequence of secularism is atheism," but he added that, "clearly all secularists are not atheists." Is we agree that secularism may imply atheism it is only for eonvenience sake and so that we may see how far this form of unbelief is receding from men's minds. During recent years I have often met in the Christian literature I come across with the same idea, I have heard it given from the pulpit frequently, and I have thought to myself, "what blindness ! Do these writers sad preachers really believe that because Mr. Bradlaugh is dead, and Mr. Holyoake is quiet, that therefore Hero- worship is dead, and unbelief is receding." Now what is the position? Just this. The vulgar unbelief of the past is the respetable and creditable belief of to-day. Has it been unbelief or belie& that has driven cal vinism with its idiotic predestination to the wall? I can well re- member with what feelings I first road Simpson's " Plea for Religion." E'er I wondered and wondered again, how it came about that all the clever scholars whose names I met with in that infamous book should he men whose lives, works, and thoughts should be nothing less than a mere preparation for hell fire. The thought was horrible. Freethieueht, or unbelief if you like, has made it possible for us to live without shaking in our shoes with fright at the Christian's bogey-man. Calls to the unconverted, and saints everlasting rests are now kuddled to the top shelves in our libraries. Voltaire, Paine, Elobbee, and the whole host of fighters for civil and religious liberty in the past were men of whom it "snot be said they are "incapable of much thought." They not only thought deeply, but they made it possible for succeeding generations of thinkers to carry on the good wark, andfnow to-day the only fighters in the theological world are the Christians themselves. The Secularists need trouble themselves no longer. Why should they, when in almost every review and monthly can be found articles written by men of " wide knowledge and capable of much thought ?" I should like to ask of Mr. Roberts two favours, and I do it in all simplicity and with a feeling that he will try to obliee. I should like him te tell me, first how many heresy trials there have been during the past ten years among the Christians of Europe and America ending with the one now pending of Professor McGiffert for his hook, " • History of Christianity in the Apostolic Age." Oi C01T35 In his answer to this question Mr. F.R. Roberts will also prove to his readers that the Christian heretics were "incapable of much thought." My next question has reference to some remarks made recently by a very shallow pated fellow known to the world as Prof. Max Muller, and given to the hero-wor- shippers of Warriugton by the" Examiner." This man " tricked out in a certain show of knowledge" told his interviewer a few of his views respecting the Bible and its contents, touching especially upon the immaculate conception and the bodily ascension of Christ. Mr. Roberts no doubt reads his " Examiner" carefully, and of course would give the column of matter to which I refer the benefit of his deep and thoughtful mind. If this ie so I beg to assure him that wa are all attention and waiting to be enlightened.—Yours truly, H. WALTHAM. 2407, Mission-st., San Francisco, Feb. 14, 1898.

div.p: BARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
EARLESTOWN ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY.

On Saturday night, in connection With the above, a social evening was held in the Town Hall, Earles- tevvn. There were about 50 couples present, and dancing was indulged in until about 11 o'clock, the music being supplied by the Society's bead.

The usual weekly meeting was held in the Co- operative Hall on Sunday afternoon, when there was again a good attendance. Mr. Markland, o 2 ewton, presided, and an address was given by Mr. Mundon, P.CiVl.,St.lielens. A recitation was given by Miss Coate. and vocal selections were contri- bused by Mr. G. Kidd.

NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTIONS. The nominations for the vacancies which will occur by rotation in the five wards of the Urban District Council are dus in on the 17th inst. The members who retire are Rev. E. W. Whittenbury- Kaye,Town Hall Ward; Mr. J. W. Emmett, Via- duct Ward ; Mr. VV.Collingwood, Wargrave Ward; Mr. C. B. F. Borron, Crow Lane Ward; Mr. F. J. Wood, Newton Ward. With the exception of the Rev. E. W. W. Kaye, all the retiring members will seek re-election, Mr. Kaye having left the district. So far as is at present known, there will be no con- test in any of the wards except Town Hall. For the vacant seat in this ward, it is rumoured there will be several candidates, but it is premature to men- tion any names. VOLUNTEER BILL AT NEWTON.

The 29th annual ball promoted by tbe G. Com- pany of the 6th V.B.K.L.R , and C. Troop of Lanca- shire Hu-sars was brought to a successful issue on Friday night in the Town Hall, Newton. Toe hall was very prettily decorated for the occasion by Mr. E. T. Evans, and presented a picturesque appear- ance with the scarlet uniforms of the Volunteers mingled with the 'note sombre dress of the hussars. There was a large number of volunteers and civilians present, amongst the officers being Commander Royse R. N., Captain Hindley-Smith, and Lieuten- ant Douglas. The music was supplied by Pearson's band and the 'LC 's were Corporals Aitken and Hill and dancing was indulged with spirit until an early hour on Saturday morning. The catering was in the hands of Mrs. Lewis, confectioner, and the liquid refreshments were supplied by Mr. llibbert.

div.head: FA AALECTOWN WOMEN'S LIERRA.L ASSOCIATION.
div.p: FA AALECTOWN WOMEN'S LIERRA.L ASSOCIATION.

Under the auspices of the above a lecture was given in the Co-operative Hall on Monday after- noon by Mrs. Eyton Jones, supplemented by an address by the Rev. elyon Jones,returned mission- ary from China. Mrs. Pis,lins presided, and there was a fairly numerous attendance. It was intended to illustrate the lecture by means of lime light views, bat through some misunderstanding al- though the lantern and screen were in readiness, it was announced that the lecturer had not brought the slides, so that this part of the programme had t 3 be omitted. The lecture consisted of an inter- esting discourse on the domestic life of the Chinese women, which she very graphically portrayed. Mr. Jones' remarks bore chiefly on the business aptitude of the Chinese and touched lightly upon Chinese politics. A large number of curios peculiar to the celestials was exhibited and aroused much interest amongst those pre,ent. At the close a vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer on the motion of Miss Greenall seconded by Miss Watson.

VIADUCT INsTITUTB BOWLING CLUB, EI.D.LESTOWN. The annual general meeting of the members of this ciub was held at the Viaduct Instituta on Mon- day evening. Mr. T. Compton presided. The minutes of the last general meeting were read and confirmed. The Secretary (Mr. W. Tarbuck), read his annual report, in which he said that the season of 1897 had been a fairly successful one, as regarded the finances. The total income for the season was £9 75., as against .E 3 133. for 1896. The expendi- ture had been a Os. CIA. and with the balance for the previous season, lth a balance of ..C4 17s. 9id. He was sorry to say that 11 of these members had run out, but they had 10 new ones, and 2 had re- joined which made the number on the books 55, against 54 in 1896. During Cie season they had played six handicaps and two home and home matches, with Rainhill and Crewe,in both of which Earlestown was successful, The report was adopte 1. It was decided to join the Newton District Bowling Association, and the Secretary and Vr. James Gee were appointed representatives. The election of officers resulted as follows :—President, Mr. Joseph Emmett; secretary, Mr. John Edgar; treasurer, Mr. James Gee; committee, 31essrs. T. Mather, G Jones, G. Butler, J. Clough, and F. Davies; captains, F. Davies, J. Gee and J. Finch : greenkeeper, J.Savage. On the motion of Mr. C. Long, seconded by Mr. J. Barlow, a vote of thanks was accorded the donor ef handicap prizes.

div.p: HOPE OP EARLESTOWN LODGE. 1.0.G.T.

On Monday evening the Pride of Earlestown Temple gave an entertainment in the Co-operative Hall. Bro. Newman, S.J.T., was in the chair. The programme opened with an ode, the following taking part in the programme :—Reading, Bro. T. Maloney; reading, Sister Frith ; reading, Bro. W Barker; recitation. Sister Frith ; reading, Bro. E. Barker ; recitation, Sister N. Newman ; piano solo, Bro. Knowles ; recitation, Sister M. Frith; recitation Bro. P. Barker; piano solo, Sister Koowles ; sister M. Kirkham in character dress then rendered" I shan't go to school any more," and Bro. E. Newman addretiPed the meeting on Good Templar, Work. The senior members then held their weekly session under the presidency of C. r., Bro. T. Cutler. A good attendance was present, and two candidates were admittei to membership. Slveral communi- cations were read by the secretary, and the Lodge Deputy, and Bro. J. Taylor gave the report of the annual district session, held at Liverpool, on Satur- day. A committee was forna.cl for the visit to the St. tlelens P,S.E , on Saturday eremitic; next, ani several discu•Aions were Srought before the lodge, dealing with the" Essay Competition." Bro Roberts of Warrington, addressed the meeting. It was de- cided to send hearty congratula'ions to the Aslatoe lodge, on their winning the " block and gavel." Afterwards the proceedings terminated.

DEATH OP VE. THOMAS PORTER.. We have this week to chronicle the death of Mr. Thomas Porter of Crow Lane, Newton, which took place at his residence on :Monday at the age of 77 years. The deceased gentleman had been in failing health for about three months, and he quietly I passed away as stated, lie was a very old resident of Newton, having been for over 50 years in the employ of MessrA. It. Evans and Co , ftrst as engine winder at Haydock, and afterwards as agent at the Newton coal depot, to which position he was ap- pointed in 1865 and held until thres years ago. lie was not by any means a public man, but he was superintendent of the Hap-lock Wesleyan Sunday School for over 20 years. HE was a life-long teeto- taller, and was one of the oldest members of the Order of Rechabitts4. He was a constant worship- per at the Earlestown Wesleyan Church and led a quiet homely life and never dabbled in public mat- ters, his favourite work bsinz in connection with temperance affairs. He leaves a widow and one son. The interment took place on Thursday after- noon at the Cemetery. Amongst those present besides the relatives, being Mr. John Fdirhurat of Haydock, an old and intimate friend, Mr. J. B. Leach of St. Helens, Mr, George Howarth, Mr. zi-tringer, and Mr. Lathom of Havilock. rhe first ' part of the burial service was read in the Wesleyan Chapel by Mr. John Plirhurst, Miss Greenall play- ing thee' Dead NI arch," as the cortege entered the chapel. At the graveside the service was completed by the Rev. F. W. Passmore.
