Tile, ACCIDENI: IN A WAiL- RINGTON BAKERY. CLA.III FUR. DAMIUES. At tile Warrington County eerier, on Monday, the hearing of the accioa brought by Stepaeu Reveascroft Turner ageless Mr9llo. James Strange and Sons, of Letehterd, claiming damages for personal iojunes sus- tained whilst in their employ ar a o ker, wee resumed before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, and a special jury. Mr. Overend Evans, and Mr. Seel of Mancneeter ' (instructed by Messrs. Jenkioa and Company) repre- sented the plaintiff, and Mr. Bradoury, ef Meuchester (instructed by Mr. F. R. R Meats) appeared fur the de- fendants. At the previous hearines of tee actioa,tbe case for the plaintiff had been put, and Mr. Bradbury now rose to address the jury on behall of toe defendante. At the outset he stated that is this case so far air any assist- ance which might have been readered to the plaintiff outside legal grounds, it was per- fectly clear that the defendants had beeu willing to give it. The plaintiff heel admitted that the defendants bad paid 10s. a week whilst he was in hoepital, and that they bed promised to mina his son on and do all they could to asaist hen. So far as an bon ourable obligation we: concerned it had been discharged by the defendant. and would have beau more thoroughly discharged if that action had not been taken. But the plaintiffeastigated perhaps by the fradee Union determined to urge his claim for conmensa- tien in a court of law on the groomed of legal liability. It was for the jury to colander the case as a strict legal claim, and co decide whether there had Hen such negligence as entitled the plaintiff to recover damages. The question for the jury to decide wan whether there was ou the part of the employers negligence with regard to Lae state of their ways, works, machinery and plant, and &madly, whether the injury to the plaintiff arose from such negligence. la o6ner words they must decide whether it was the plaintiff's fault, or through negligence, and want of care au the part of the einyloyers tnat brought about the injury. The plaintiff had got to in eke that out. Wirat Was due care? Wherever there was machinery, whatever care was taken there was some risk if men were not reasonably careful for their own safety. Machinery could not be used without some risk, and the law did not say that an ern ;toyer should feace off his machinery and take such extraordinary precautions that an accident wend not possibly happen. It said the em- ployer sheuld take such care as a reasonable man should take who had a proper regard for hie s.ervents. The case for the plaintiff had been put upon two grounds. Teeae were that the timer of bakehouse WAS wet and slippery and therefore in a dangerous stete,and secondly that the machine which was being worked Load no cover on. He could not forbear from peiunog out that it seemed very odd that if this machine was 80 dangeSOU3.that it had been working for five years with- out any accideat of any kind happeningefnere had been no change in the machine, different men had worked it, and no accidhnt had occurred. Did it not rather point to this, that if a m ichine could be used for five years without accident, something unusual occurred on this particular occasion? With regard to the allegation that the leer near the machinery was sKppery,the defendants did not deny that there was eotrie drip from the bearings but it was so small that it could have been guarded against if the plaintiff had taken reasonable care. Tne only witness who spoke to the state of the floor at the time of the accident was the plaintiff. His evidence was that the floor was wet, but in this he Was not corrooor- ated by the policemen who visited the bakehouse imme- diately after the accident. He (Mr.Bradbury)would call overwhelming evidence that the floor was dry.lt was the plaintiff's duty to see to the floor being swept, and he (etr.Bradbury) ventured to say that this was a trumped up sort of negligence which had been brought forward by the plaintiff with the object of making out a case if he could. Addressing the jury with reference to the question of a cover for the machine,Mr. Bradbury asked them after having seen the machine whether they thought it was such a machine that any employer would think ought to he fenced and guarded so that a man could not tumele into it and have his hand cut off? He contended that if a cover was necessary to the machine, every machine in Warrington ought to be covered. One of the plaintiff's witnesses named Wright who had worked the machine for years, said there was no need for a cover. The case was absurdly weak on this point. The plaintiff bed worked this machine years ago, and he did not venture to say that he had ever suggested to his employer that it required a cover. THE PROCEE-DINGS ON THURSDAY. The further hearing of the case was continued on Thursday, Frederick Bancroft was the first witness called. He stated that he was a baker, and lived at Hewitt-st. had been In the employ of the defendants since last March. He was now the second hand in the bake- house, Mr. liindley being the first hand. Mr. Taylor did not now work for the defendants. Witness was the secend hand last Oatobsr, and occasioaally he had worked the machine. From his experience there was no danger in working the machine. He tild not nit* it required a cover to make it safe. Ile had no- ticed that a little water dripped from the bottom bearing on the left-hand side of the machine. In order to catch the drip,a bread tin was place] underneath. Weeen the tin was attended to there was no necessity fn. water on the floor; it was only a small quantity that dripped. Toe tin was emptied an a week, but it would take a fort- algid: to fill it. There was no wet on the floor wen the accident happened. Witness was working with tom plaintiff and Taylor on the night in question, and they were mixing the third "batch" when the accident occurred. The machine was scraped after the last nailing and if they did a little pre- liminary scraping before the dough was turd s I out it saved titre. Witeess had eeeta the plaintiff scraping the machine before the operation was completed on other occasions. They went home as soon as their work was done. The sooner the kneading was dcleflt,the earlier would they be able to get home. Oa the night of 0 :tober 11th he saw tho plaintiff standing by the machine during the kne ding of the tWrd batch. The plaintiff was scraping the machine, and he told witness to go upstairs and put some lour down, and instructed Taylor with reference to the tins. Witness went upstairs and it took about two minutes to put the flour down. He heard Turner shout, and when he came down in the bekehouse ho saw that Turner was without his hand. Witness immediately want and stopped the machine. Taylor ran out for assistance, and witness led Turner to a seat, and brought him a drink of water. Taylor returned in company with a policeman. After Turner bat been taken tip the Infirmary witness looked into the machine, and saw the plaintiff's hind grasping a scraper. Witness lifted the scraper out of the machine. It had some flesh and blood upon it, and wit- ness placed it on a table. The hand was partly buried in the dough, the fingers obtruding.—Cross-exansined : Witness was employed at the bakehouse with Wright. He had seen the floor of the bakehouse wet in consequence of the spillimg of water which was being carried to the , machine. The tin had run over on two or three occa- sions. He had seen a sack placed on the floor, to keep the feet dry, It eiould also preveut The floor was riot wet at the time of the accident. He noticed it after Turner had departed for the Infirmary. There was nothing but blood on the floor. The tin was emptied on the previous Tuesday. He saw Turner scrape the machine when in motion cm the previous Sunday nieht. When hey were waiting they sometimes lay down for a rest. The engine was upstairs,and the only machine in the bakeheuse was the kneading machine. There were other machines upstairs. P C, Monks was in bekehouie when witness picked the scraper out of the machine. The scraper lay on the top of the band. The blade of the scraper was bent a little crossways. The Wood and flesh were chiefly on the blade of the scraper When Monks took the bend out,witness said "Here's the scraper." Witness denied that be told Wright that the dough brought the hand round to the top, and that he took it sum, with the scraper sticking to it. On the 23rd October Mrs. Turraer spoke to him in company with Taylor and said " When you emptied the dough out of the machine did VOL find anything besides the hand ?'' Witme,s replied "Yea, the scraper; it was gripped in the hand ; it was covered with blood,and Taylor cleaned it." —Re-examined by Mr. Bradbury : From the beginning he had told everybody who asked him that he Look the scraper out of the machine. He had not varied it in ths least. He thuueht Wright had been trying to get evi- dence. The tin was about half full when he emptied it on the Tuesday prior to the accident. The hand was not cat up at all. He considered tue photograph pro duced a correct one of the machine.

div.p: Mr. Evans objected to the photograph without the photographer was called. John Strange said he was an amateur photographer, arid the phatograph produced was of the machine in quesion. The machine was three feet from side to side.

William Henry flawkslev.now residing at Stockport,a foreman baker. said he was working for the defendants irs November,l392,when the machine was put down. He was the foreman,and he began to work the machine. In his opinion there was not the slightest danger in working the machine. He had seen similar machines working at other places,and had not seen one with a cover. There Wag no danger to a sen,ible man in working the machine without one.—Croip-exatnined : There was no drip whatever wh•n he worked it. A small man had tu stand on a rail of the mt.:him) in order to reach the shutter when letting down the flour. He-examined : Tnere was no danger in that to a caretul man. This concluded the case for the defendants.

Ur. Overend Evans then addressed the jury for the plaintiffs. Referring to the last witness Mr. Evans said he did not help the defendants retail because at that time the machine WWI hr parfect order. Proceeding to refer to the danger which attended a workman when he was obliged to stand on a rail of the machine iii order to reach the shutter he said it was absurd to say th•t there was no dAn4er to the workman.

Ntr. kiradbury ['his is not alleged as a danger. The only causes alleged are the cover and the water. Mr. Evans has no right to introduce this matter. Mr. Evans : I suzgest that I have 45 an exarrnol.. to show that the defendants haven't been careful to pre- vent their workmen from accident.
Ws Honour: lam afraid you are restricted by the terms of your particulars. Mr. Evans: I don't deny that. His Honour : You cannot go into thl general subject as to the danger of the machine.

Mr. Evans : The negligence is certainly based on the want of a cover and the elipoery state of the floor. lam not trying to get out of that, and I ant somewhat bound by those particulars. Prooeeding, Mr. Evans said Mr. Bradbury went fully into the case and took considerable time to do it. His friend began his remarks by refer- ence to the fact that the defendants had shown that they were willing to meet this man and allowed him 10s. a week. But that came to nothing at all ;it was an act of grace on the part of the defendants. In connection w:th the Employers Liability Act the plaintiff was bound to give notice of his claim within six weeks of the acci- dent. The evidence of Mrs. Turner was that she asked Mr. Jams Strange to put in writing what he intended to do. N)thine came of that, and as a consequence the matter could not be left any I ,nger in abeyance. If the plaintiff had done so the defendants would have been able to snao their fingers at him, and he would have to whistle for his rem-dy un icr thn Ernployors Lisoility Act. It was not likely that the dermdanta would admit their liability and allow the plaintiff the sum a f money he was entitle] to. The action was brought with regard to the two matters in which they alleged the deteadaa's had been neglieent. The plaintiff con- tended that the machine ought not to be worked without a cover, and that the floor on this par- t;celar night was slippery thrnets the negligencee of the defendants. With regard to the want of a cover the lure had heard rivhlPtle'-t that Meesre. Lunt,of Liver- pool, worked their machines with covers and Mr. Balcarriet, who was called by the defendants, said that if there was plenty of head room it wa3 a desirable tking to have a cover wi h the object of saving the fl tar. But the manager from Messrs. Lunt stated that it was covered with the object of guarding the workmen against accident, and if that were ro then the defendants w re nut entitled to say that their premises were unsuited to them. It did not help them o say that they would have to provide another system of adding the water to the flour. It was necessary to pro, ct the workmen even if it entailed the expense ot proeiding a fresh system of supplying the machine with water. It was an entirely different thing for his friend, Mr. Bradbury, to :Levee, that it would be necessary to guard a workmen when you placed a knife into his heed, because it was a dangerous thing. The defendant's macnine was is sort of mill which if you once got into it you could not get Out without loss of limb or life. If a machine was dangerous a master was not entitled to go on working it unless he was prepared to compensate the workman for any injury he might receive. Then with regard to the state of the floor there had been a mass of evi- dence wish reference to that. He submitted that he had made out that the floor on the nccasion of the accident was in a slippery condition. Ho had been able to call before them several witnesses The plaintiff had told them that he called Mr. Strange's attention to its wet condition. Then there was the witness Wrient wile stated that the drip did not only come from the bearing on the left hand side hut also from the others, and that he found it necessary to place tins on each side of the machine. He also told them that in order to protect himaelf from slipping he was obliged to put a sack down. There was another witness named CarflAd who was called by the defendants and who spoke as to the wet condition of the floor. It was even admitted by the defendants that the machine leaked,and it was certain that the bearings would tend to get worse with wear, and that the leakage would increase. Under such circumstances the floor must have been in a sloppy condition. The plaintiff did his duty in the matter by calling the attention of the defendants to it, and it then became their duty to see that the lives and limbs of their workanea were not risked. The defendants bad tried to prove that the plaintiff ought to have seen to the matter himself, but their witness Cortield stated that there was not always time to see to the tin, and that it sometimes overflo wed.

Mr. Bradbury : Be said distinctly that when three mem were in the bakehouse there was no difficulty in emptying the tin. Mr. Evans : He said nothing of the kind. It was oh- viout that the men hadn't time to attend to the empty- ing of the tin. The machine not only leaked at one point but at all four bearings,and he submitted that the prac- tice of putting a can to catch the drippings was not an efficient way of dealing with the matter. Proceeding to give the history of the accideet,Mr.Evani Said the plain. tiff's hand was cut off during the third batch. The plaintiff had told them how he got his hand taken off- One witnesa catjed by the defendant said that it was im- possible for a man to get his hand cut off. It was non- sense to say that a machine of this kind could not be so dangerous. The jury knew what happened. Bancroft had stated that he took the scraper from the top of the dough. It was a curious thing that Monks,who was in the bakehouse at the time saw no scraper taken out of the machine. His (Mr. Evans') suggestion with regard to that was that the scraper was taken out of the mac- hine when it was necessary to clean it of the dough. Mr. Bradbury had put it that the scraping of the machine whilst in motion WAS done to save a little time, so that the men would be able to get away earlier. One witness had stated that the plaintiff had even scraped the blades whilst in motion, but he (Mr. Evana) eaggested that it was impeseible to du that, and further that it was use- less to do so beettise the next moment the blades would be in the dough again, and cyrored with it. LI seemed ridiculous to suggest anything of the kind. Dealing with the statement that the scraper was found in the dough, he pointed out that if the scraper had been in the machine at that time it would have been mangled.- They must remember that the hand was pliable and ceuld accommodate itself, but the scraper was rigid and would be crushed by the blades of the machine. He suggested that the scraper had never been in the machine or the handle would have been smashed. It was impossible for the scraper to be in the position stated by Bancroft. He suggested that that witness was not telling the truth when he said be took the scraper out of the machine. The plaintiff was not working the scraper at all at the time his hand was caught. If it were true they would have found a different state of things with segard to the scraper. Toe handle would have bem,in a different con- dition as it was made of wood and would easily have been smashed to pieces. Bancroft had told two different Stories with reference to the manner he found the scraper. Mr. Evans next dealt with the statement of the plaintiff that Mr. William Strange told him to clue that he was using the scraper at the time of the accident He peinted out that it would have produced a bad effect if the customers of the defendant's had thought that the blood and matter from the defendant's hand had been mixed up with the dough. The policemen did not go in far as to say that Mr. William Strange did not speak to the plaintiff, and it was possible that in the excitement and confusion it might escape their observation. Mr. William Strange had stated that he never spoke to the plaiutiff at all. But what did the jury think of that? Mere was a man who had been in their employ for souse time, and yet Mr. William Strange wished thorn to be- lieve that he never asked the man how it happened and never spike a single word ta him. It was not in the nature of things, and it seemed to suggest that he was afraid of the circumstances being known. In order to deny the story of the plaintiff Mr. William Strange rather overdid it,end he thought it would make the jury regard his evidence as worthless. The plain tiff's statement was confirmed somewhat by the boy poeev, who was told by William Strange to tell the cus- tomers that the plaintiff had got his hand taken off by the cogwheela. The explanation of the remarks made by the plaintiff at the Infirmary were due to the iestiga- tion of Mr. William Strange. The wituesses called had misunderstood or misinterpreted the plahatiff's words inasmuch as they were not familiar with the circum stances. He Was unable to call witnesses from the Infirmary on behalf of the plaintiff because the state- ments were made in t e absence of the defendants, and therefore they could not go into the box. That placed him in a very awkward position. The defendants were entitled to call witnesses,end yet there might be twenty others in 'pposition to them,and they could not be called by the plaintiff. .

_ His Honour : It is not quite fair to tiring that tor. ward. That is the law, and you ought nap to complain to the jury. Mr. Evans sugrsted that he was entitled to do to. In rhomands of c4,a complaints had been made again and again of the unfair state of the law on this point. No difficulty arose with regard to the evidence of the patients who were at the Infirmary, it the jary were saltisfied that Mr. William Strange told the plaintiff to make the statement with reference to the scraper. Deal- ing with the question of damages which the plaintiff was entitled to recover. Mr. Evans stated that they were assessed on the rate of wages paid for that particular

employment in the district, and three years wages were allowable. It had been proved in evicience that Taylor who was promoted to first hand received £2 a week,and he would suggest to the jury that that advancement I had been a strong influence in inducing Taylor to come forward and give evidence. In conclusion he asked the jury to find a verdict in favour of the plaintiff. His Honour summed up at great length,occupying the atteation of the jury for over three hours. He reviewed the evidence on both sides, and called the particular attention of the jury to the statements mada by the plaintiff whilst an inmate of the Infirmary. He said it was suggested that the statements were made at the in- stigation of William Strange, with a view to preventing any Injury to their trade. According to that argument all that the witnesses front the Infirmary had said might be true,but the statements made entirely false and at the suggestion of William Strange. Considerable comment had been made as to the probability that William Strange would make the statement attributed to him. It was denied by William Strange that he did so,zed he daresay the jury would think that if William Strange did tell the plaintiff to make these statements it was a very wicked thing to do. It was inducing the plaintiff to tell a lie upon a material circumstance affecting himself. If the jury thonght William Strange did make use of the statement, they must give proper weight to it. It was rather a serious charge to tnakr, and the jury must not lightly accede to the suggestion. Dilating on the evidence with respect to the state of the floor, his Honour pointed out to the jury that they must consider that the plaintiff was the foreman with two men under him who were to obey his orders. If the plaintiff saw that the floor was wet and slippery why didn't he tell the assistants to wipe it up ? It was his duty to order , them to do so,and to see that it was done. It the plain- tiff neglected to do so, then the fault was the plaintiff's and not the defendant's. The evidence with regard to the lack of a cover far the machine tended to show that the'plaintiff never complained of the working of the machine, and did not ask for a cover. If Wright could , put dawn a sack of four, and use the machine daily without a cover, why could not the plaintiff? A man would have no right to put his he td in the fire because there was no guard to it. If tile jury thought that ' the plaintiff had sustained this injury through the negligence of the defendants in not providing a cover or in not having the bearings repaired so as to prevent the drip, and they thought the defendants did not take pre- cautions, their verdict must be for the plaintiff. The jury must be quite cleftr on the question of negligence, and that the plaintiff did' not contribute to it. If they believed the witnewes from the Infirmary, and that Mr. William Strange did not go into the bakehouse and make the suggestion alleged, then they must give a verdict for the defendants. . .
_ After a short deliberation in private,the jury returned into Court and the foreman (Mr. William Gill) announced that they had decided on a verdict for the defendants.

An open meeting of the above Was held on Sun- day at the Y.M.C.A. Lecture Hall,which was crowded, many being unable to gain admittance. The chair was occupied by Mt. T. Cowdell, who give a brief address. Mr. Levi Richardson sang " But thou did'st not leave" (Handel) in a finished mannerond Mr. W. J. Ashton gave a recitation, entitled " The Lifeboat" in good sty le. The speaker for the day was Mr. Silcock,whose address was listened to with great attention. The characteristic heartiness of the meeting and singing made another brief,bright, and brotherly serv:ce. Mr. F. Hickman,Mr.Jenkins and Mr. E. Taylor also took part in the meeting. LECTURE AT STRETTON.

The last lecture of a series on agriculture was given in the schoolroom Stretton on Monday even- ing, by Mr. W. Edwards, lecturer, appointed by the County Council. There was again a large attend- ance of farmers and others interested in the subject which was " Gr3wth and management of root crops." The chair was occupied by Mr. J. C, Parr, J. , D.L. Mr. Edwards treated the subject in a thoroughly practical manner, and his remarks were attentavelY listened to. An animated discussion took place afterwards,a hearty vote of thanks being passed in the usual way to Mr. Edwards for his able lecture and to the chairman for presiding. The lectures have been well attended, and sound prac- tical adviesi has been given

INDUSTRI&L BRANCH.—The Premiums received during the year were £4,793,591, being an increase of £214,798. The Claims of the year amounted to £1,823,338. The number of Free Policies granted during the year to those Policy-holders of five years' standing, who desired to diseontinue their payments was 60,848, the number in force being 549,889. The number of Free Policies which became Claims during the year was 10,716. The total number of Policies in force at the end of the year was 12,546,132 : their average duration exceeds eight and a quarter years.
